utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May I raise one matter at this stage? It concerns the time available to the accused for cross-examination. This is obviously a very important witness. We appreciate that there has become a witness congestion problem for the Prosecution. That was not the accused's responsibility nor fault. The witness that was preceding this witness in terms of the case was not of such importance. The Prosecution time was quite a sufficient period that has eaten into the time for this witness. I appreciate he was taken fairly swiftly by Mr. Groome in something under two hours, but it has had the unfortunate effect of reducing the amount of time available to the accused if other witnesses are sought to be fitted in today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll think about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. You can have an extra half hour. You've got an hour and a quarter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Selak, we left off yesterday discussing the attack on the military column of the JNA in Dobrovoljacka Street. I'm sure you will remember the event and several officers were killed on the occasion, among them a woman who was also in the column, a young soldier, and the rest were transferred to the Dom and the gym where the members of the military police of the Patriotic League interrogated them and so on. I'm sure you're aware of the event. Yes?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this event, Your Honours. However, I don't know the details of it, so I can't testify to that because I don't know the real truth of what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was the source of your information about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The information media, the radio, the television, the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. No point asking him about what he read in the papers. I'm going to interrupt you for one minute, Mr. Milosevic. There is a matter which we should have dealt with -- I should have dealt with at the outset to assist the Prosecution involving witness B-1047, who is going to give evidence soon. This is an application to admit his evidence in lieu of viva voce under Rule 92 bis. We have seen the objections raised by the amicus. We uphold those objections. We do so for two reasons. First of all substantive, that this is a witness giving evidence about a new municipality, Sanski Most, and a new incident in it. It is important evidence. We think it should be given live. Secondly, procedural, that it is out of time, and we said on the last occasion that we gave a ruling that we would regard such matters with care and would by no means necessarily give leave if applications were made out of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, and do you know that it was precisely because of those events, the time you were still in active service, the blockades, the attacks on the column, and so on that the officers, their families, and soldiers from other republics were transported by air from Sarajevo, Banja Luka, Tuzla, to Yugoslavia? They were flown to Yugoslavia precisely because of those attacks. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, that wasn't only because of the attack. It was that people from Croatia, Serbs from Croatia were travelling to Bosnia and Serbia, and they were being transported by planes and by cars and also by railway. I know that because from Banja Luka, you would either take a plane or some other means of transport. So in addition to the families leaving, they would take their property with them too, their movables.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that the officers who were originally from Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia had the right to decide, after the 15th of May, whether they would like to remain in their own republics and be placed at the disposal of their peoples, that was their right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody stated what they wanted to do individually. I know that from my particular unit not a single Serb and Montenegrin -- born in Serbia and Montenegro did not ask to leave their positions in Banja Luka, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean from your logistics base?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, from Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the whole of Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the corps command. I know about that. I don't know about the individual units so I don't want to talk about that. I don't want to testify about the individual cases I don't know about. But as to the corps command and the command of the base, I do know that and I do know that not a single officers or non-commissioned officer wanted to return or left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's something you claim, but let's move on. We'll come to that. In the 1996 statement, you say that it became clear from 1991 that non-Serb officers cannot be trusted and that they weren't welcome. This is on page 6. Now, do you have, as I see that you have various data available to you, do you happen to know how many Muslims there were in the army of Republika Srpska at all?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got any information exact information as to the officer cadres who were Muslims or Croats by ethnicity in the army of Republika Srpska, but yesterday when we -- we were discussing that matter, and there was some misunderstanding that arose. It was considered that I remained in the army of Republika Srpska. Your Honours, I did not. On the 18th of May, 1992, there was official proclamation of the army of Republika Srpska. Whereas on the 19th of May I tabled my request for retirement, and the General Staff, the administrative department did in fact retire me, accepted my request. So I was no longer an officer of the army of Republika Srpska. My officers, Croats and Bosniaks from the base, that is to say nine of them, I think it was nine of them, left the logistics base and went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And later on, they had to go to other states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume they went to other states of their own free will, didn't they, other countries?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because they feared for their lives if they were to stay in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And I have a concrete case in point where a man saved his life and he now lives in Ireland. His name is Captain Tako Redzep [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, were any of the officers killed from the former JNA when they went to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia? Can you quote a single example of any case of that kind?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no information about that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm glad to hear that at least, that you say you don't know. But you're saying now that you didn't remain yourself. You didn't stay on and that there was a misunderstanding when it came to you. I didn't claim that you stayed on in Republika Srpska and the army. I said quite the contrary, that you were at the head of some secret organisation, Muslim one, in Banja Luka and you confirmed that yourself.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Muslim, of the Banja Luka people, Bosniaks and Croats who feared for their lives, and people were fleeing, and we advised them to leave and save their lives because there was a lot of arrests and abuses and beatings, corpses were thrown into the Vrbas River and so on and so forth. So we advised the people to escape from Banja Luka if they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Selak. In your 1996 statement, you say that to the end of 1992, Muslim officers and Croats were replaced who held posts of leadership in the army such as the commanders of brigades, platoons, regiments, and so on.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an order issued by General Mladic, and I have it, Your Honours, here with me. I think the OTP has it as well. And that order orders Muslims and Croats to be replaced from their duties and to be sent to the army of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia for further disposition. That was May, I think, 1992. The order was a May order of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is probably something that refers to individual cases, but for example, do you happen to know about this, that the 2nd Semberija Brigade, Paso Halilovic [phoen] was in command of that particular brigade, do you know about that? And throughout the war he was the commander, so I'm asking you very specifically.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hearing the name of that man for the first time. I've never heard of him before. I don't know about his name or the post he occupied, so I can't comment because I don't know the man.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just quoting an example which denies -- refutes what you've just said.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Individual cases are not the general rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quite agree with that except that you were speaking about individual cases yourself. Now, do you know that to a great measure Croats and Muslims from the JNA left because they wanted to of their own free will, and for the most part they would join up the newly established military formations that were created on ethnic grounds in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Is that true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not true, Your Honours, because yes, there were paramilitary formations, yes there were volunteer units, and the JNA officially supported these and appointed officers and supplied them with weapons and materiel. There is official data to bear that out. But, Your Honours, I would like once again to refer to the order by the commander of the army of Republika Srpska, General Ratko Mladic, who under number 28/4 of the 9th of June orders and I quote: "To the officers -- that officers, Muslims and Croats, should be sent on leave straight away, forthwith, and that they should be sent to the army of Yugoslavia in order to deal with their status in the service." And it was on the basis of this order that people did indeed leave and go to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. And this was strictly confidential.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you yourself said nothing happened to them; is that right? When they arrived in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But they had reason to leave the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and go to third states.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's not true. They didn't leave all of them. But you weren't listening to go my question. I said that the Muslims and Croats mostly -- the majority of them, left the JNA and joined up with the other units, the Muslims and Croats, Croat units. You said paramilitary units, but I said that the Croats and Muslims left the JNA to form the newly established formations which were formed on an ethnic basis in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you've answered that question. You said no, it's not true. Now, let's have another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How come that 1.100 officers, officers of the former JNA, found themselves in the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina then?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what should they have done, Your Honours? They had to defend their own people or should they have left them to be slaughtered? The result of this was had this not happened, there would have been even more victims and unfortunately, as I said, 287.000 were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you about the facts and you are now expounding on those facts. So what I'm saying is true, is it not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is true that the people -- these officers joined the army to defend their own people. And I fully agree with that. I approve. I couldn't go myself because I was prohibited from leaving Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am just noting and observing what you said, and we can make a whole image from the different mosaic pieces of how these individual armies were formed in this process.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you, Milosevic, gave over the whole of the JNA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't address --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- handed it over --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't address the accused, please, Mr. Selak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I was saying, in your statement you also claim and state that the officers, like all the others who stepped over to the new Yugoslav army in the SRY -- FRY, were given very low-ranking positions because people didn't trust them. That was not true.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was true, Your Honours, and I have cases to quote as examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We went over this yesterday. I don't think we need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 1996, you say that the units of the Banja Luka Corps were engaged in Croatia. So now I'm asking you the following. Do you know that according to the report of the command of the Argentine and Nepalese battalions respectively in the UN, the army of Republika Srpska was not engaged in Western Slavonia, and the last soldier was withdrawn from there around the 5th of June, 1992, as well as the command of the 5th Corps of the JNA from Stara Gradiska. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the units withdrew in the month of July but the tanks remained preserved there and weapons did as well. I'm talking about the KP Dom in Stara Gradiska and Croatia and that was guarded by the army. I know that there were ten tanks there, T34 self-propelled transporters and also artillery weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, please answer my questions. Oh, let me get closer to the microphone. I'm being told by the interpreters that they can't hear me. And do you know that the main task of the JNA at the time was the creation of buffer zones between the conflicting parties and the mobilisation of the JNA and the TO which was under the command of the JNA according to the constitution of the SFRY and the law on People's Defence and also on the protection of military facilities? Is that right, Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was official policy, but that was not the way people behaved in practice. So it was practice that refuted this altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Selak, in your statement -- oh, I see. So you're saying that official policy was one thing and in practice other things happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know about that the best, because you issued orders for that kind of thing, and you imposed such solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Selak. I was on official policy and you are talking about some official policy?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You took over the army -- the control over the army in June 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Selak. You cannot testify about that. That's for sure. In your statement, on page 11 you say that there is a list of members of the Banja Luka Corps who are responsible for the war, as you put it, and for the atrocities that were committed by members of the corps. On the basis of what are you accusing these people when you know full well what their duty was of each and every one of these officers in the corps?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, these are people who are responsible for carrying out genocide in the territory of Bosanska Krajina, especially in the municipalities of Prijedor, Sanski Most, Kotor Varos, Bosanska Gradiska and other municipalities. That is precisely what I spoke about. I talked about their responsibility for having carried out genocide. About 2.000 people were killed in one day in Kozarac, and it is these people who are responsible for all these crimes in the mentioned municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to get to that, and it's somewhat different from the way you've put it or, rather, it is quite different. And on page 8, in the last paragraph you even deal with the reasons for the war. You say that the three main reasons for the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina are Serb nationalism, propaganda of the Serbian Orthodox Church, and the propaganda of the Serb academy of sciences and arts. That is what you said, Mr. Selak; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, since you are delving into all these issues, mainly issues you don't know about, tell me, is it correct that this war in Bosnia-Herzegovina started when at the referendum, without the participation of the Serb people, an illegal decision was reached on the independence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, although it is a fact that the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina said that the republican consists of three peoples who had equal rights according to the constitution. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. Your Honours, the Serb people in their referendum in October 1991 stated that they wanted to stay behind in Yugoslavia. And at the referendum on the 29th of February and on the 1st of March, 1992, they did not vote en masse. They simply did not take part in the vote. Sixty per cent of those who voted at the referendum voted in favour of an independent sovereign Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which was recognised by the European Union and by the United Nations, and that is the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the tragedy of it all, that this recognition led to the conflicts that took place later. Do you remember that the main foreign representatives at that time who were dealing with Yugoslavia-related issues, namely Cyrus Vance and Lord Carrington indicated that recognition before having all three peoples accede to it would mean the beginning of a civil war? Do you remember these warnings? Do you remember these facts, these facts which are undeniable, and after all, recorded in their public statements?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that Karadzic stated --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you whether you remember this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What does it matter what this witness knew or didn't know? It could be something he read in the papers. Again, it cannot assess the Tribunal to hear, quite honestly, with respect to him his views about it. Now, have you got some more concrete questions which the witness can deal with it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, he is specifically talking about the reasons for the war, and I'm asking him about what the actual reasons for the war are. So I'm asking him on the basis of his statement. It's not that I'm making up new questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He didn't give any evidence about this, as I recollect. And really, it's not a matter for him what started the war. All he can tell us about is what was happening in Banja Luka and his experience. His general views, I'm afraid to say, are totally irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. What he wrote in these statements of his are irrelevant matters; right? So there's no need for me to question him about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If he did give them in evidence, yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since you're talking about the independence of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is it correct that the decision was passed without the presence of Serbian members of parliament in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The members of parliament from the ranks of the Serb people, Your Honours, left the session of parliament of their own free will. They obstructed the debate on this issue within parliament. That is what I do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that Alija Izetbegovic, who did not hide his ambitions to create a state of an Islamic orientation --

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you present in the debates at the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Were you a member of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. All irrelevant, Mr. Milosevic. Now, let's move on to something he can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right. Then I'm not going to ask him. But he did talk about his own explanations of the reasons that led to the war, and now you're saying that I can't ask him about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. I'm going to stop you because you are misunderstanding the point. The views of witnesses about why historical events happened are irrelevant. Now, it may be necessary at some stage for us to rule on it, but we shall do so on the evidence of those who can give evidence about it. If you want to give evidence about it, you can, if you think you can assist us. But the views of the base commander in Banja Luka at the relevant time, with due respect to him, are not relevant to these proceedings. That's the point. So you debate -- try and debate with these witnesses all these political points. It's all totally irrelevant, and you'll be stopped. Ask them about their evidence. And if they say -- if they give views in statements, then that is not evidence unless it's given in court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. All right, Mr. May. It is political issues that are being tried here, nothing else. What have I got to do with everything he's been testifying about anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But tell me now that these tensions that existed, that were present during the referendum throughout the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina culminated in the killing of Nikola Gardovic, a Serb, and the wounding of Radenko Mirovic, also a Serb, and this is on the 1st of March and it was during a wedding?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've been told that you are not to ask him questions. Now, if you waste more time by not obeying instructions, the whole cross-examination will be brought to an end. It's up to you whether you want to go on or not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I am dealing with the things that the witness talked about in relation to various events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the attack on the military convoy in Tuzla that was withdrawing from that town and when 49 soldiers were killed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I heard about this particular incident over the media as well, and I don't want to make any comments because I haven't got any accurate information. I'm testifying under oath, and I don't want to do any wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know about the directive that pertained to all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Izetbegovic issued this directive to the Main Staff of the TO for an all-out attack against all JNA barracks. You were a soldier then. This was the 12th of April, 1992. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the first time I hear of this document. I did not have it in my hands, and I never heard a word about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Selak. In your statement, on page 10, paragraph 1, you say that municipal leaders wanted to be protected from paramilitary formations and mistreatment that was carried out by the SOS. And then it says in brackets "Serb defence forces." And that these SOS were political and police forces of the Serb Democratic Party that did work for them. Now, tell me, since this is what you allege, who commanded this SOS? You allege this is what happened. Who commanded these forces?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was head of the group for -- for cooperation with the UN, my offices were in the Bosna Hotel. On the first floor in the same hotel were paramilitary formations, or rather, the headquarters of the Red Berets. And the White Eagles and others were in Banja Luka. They were even selling weapons at the Kozara barracks. I noted this in my official notebook, that paramilitary formations are selling weapons in the Kozara barracks, and their headquarters were in the Hotel Bosna and they had their training grounds at Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who are these Red Berets, please?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are military formations of the Serb Democratic Party that were assisted by the Yugoslav People's Army. There is documentation here about them in the OTP where this is approved, that is to say to set up such organisations as forces of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's add this to the list then. So you claim that the Serb Democratic Party had Red Berets of their own; right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had their own paramilitary formations. That's for sure. That's something I know and there are documents to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you say that paramilitary units trained at Manjaca, is it correct that General Talic, at the meeting held in March 1992 ordered all paramilitary formations to leave the Manjaca training grounds?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the month of May when a camp for prisoners of war was established at Manjaca. He issued an order to establish this kind of camp for 2.500 men, and then he had to withdraw the paramilitaries from their training grounds in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it's not that he abolished them altogether, it was for this detention centre for prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what the war book says. I'm not going to comment on his orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Manjaca is often referred to, and I heard this when I came here. Is it correct, the information that I received, that this centre for prisoners of war went on for a total of about three months?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. On the 1st of June while reporting to the corps commander, and I was present, he ordered the establishment of a camp for prisoners of war at Manjaca. The commander of the camp was Bozidar Popovic, then a lieutenant colonel and then a full colonel. The camp went on until the 18th of December 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When was it established? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the month of June. The orders were received on the 1st of June and I was in Manjaca on the 12th of June and I was dealing with logistics, and I saw inmates in barns because, actually, this was a cattle farm. So they were preparing the premises for taking in prisoners of war who ranged from the age of 15 up to 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it went on for longer than three months?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said from June to December.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that is about six months. And did anybody mistreat prisoners of war there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not only that they mistreated them, they killed them. I haven't got the names here, but I do have them in Sarajevo in my notebook, the names of persons who were killed in Manjaca. I know about 11 people who were killed in Manjaca. I have their names, and they originally come from Kljuc and Sanski Most most of them. I do have these names, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right then, since you were there, since you saw the prisoners of war and now you say that you have some names, did you see anybody mistreat a prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see that because I was officially touring the logistics. I only saw inmates, men who were building a fence around the barns. I did not go in, and I did not check out the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You said a few minutes ago that you're testifying under oath and that you don't want to speak about things you are not aware of; then please stick to what you saw yourself.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said what I saw, and I stand by that. There were people who were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what you said in relation to Colonel Bozidar Popovic is something that you also heard from someone? Is that right? You didn't see him do that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I knew him. He was my neighbour where I lived in Banja Luka and I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You know him. Did he tell you about that? Did he tell you that he killed some prisoners of war? Did he tell you about that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Your Honours, I never said that, that he did any of the killing, but people under his command were killing people. And of course he is responsible for having allowed that as camp commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure he allowed it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I believe that no comment is required in this respect, because it is only natural that a commander is responsible for actions taken by his subordinates and he did not take any sanctions against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you sure he did not take any sanctions if something happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was the Red Cross there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Red Cross did come there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Will you explain, please, since in your statement, this is the statement of 2000, on page 8, in the fifth paragraph, you say that you're not sure how members of paramilitary units were being armed at Manjaca; is that right? You yourself say that you're not sure, that you don't know what happened, but you put it in your statement?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, allow me to explain this. In the November, I was in the office of the corps commander who at the time was General Uzelac. Colonel Subotic called him up on the phone. He was later army Minister of Republika Srpska, and he asked him about the training of paramilitary units at Manjaca, of non-military organisations. And later on, General Uzelac asked me what was the first name of Subotic. He didn't know his first name. Subotic used to be assistant chief at the military academy for logistics, and he personally organised the training of paramilitary formations at Manjaca. I know this because I know Subotic very well, and he told me that. He said that there were people being trained who were not from the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they members of the TO?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. They were not the TO. I said that the headquarters of those formations was at the Bosna Hotel in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I quoted you saying that you didn't know how they were armed, and you also go on to say that you didn't know which groups were being trained there nor who was the commander, because you personally didn't witness that training.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, at the -- on the 1st of June when we were briefing General Talic, he ordered that all the soldiers at Manjaca be armed. I have that note here in this notebook, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So he ordered the soldiers to be armed.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that they be given weapons. That soldiers be given weapons. He said "soldiers." Of course he wouldn't say civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He used the term "soldiers." But you believed they were civilians.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they were paramilitary units, because there was no need for him to explain that to us. We gathered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you didn't see any of that, let us finish with Manjaca. You don't know which units were there, nor how they were armed, nor who was their commander. You didn't see any of that yourself, did you? Is that right, Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't go to Manjaca later on to watch the training, but the information of the corps commander and his order was explicit, and it explained everything, that the people who were being trained at Manjaca should be armed and pulled out of Manjaca so that the prisoners of war could be accommodated there. Where they went after that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of the decree of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina issued on the 8th of April when the republican staff of the TO was abolished and the staff of the TO of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was formed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of that order. I don't know the details, but I do know of the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that by that same order the president relieved of duty General Lieutenant Colonel Drago Vukosavljevic was relieved of his duty and Hasan Efendic appointed Staff Commander?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know that. I didn't have that order in my hand. I was in Banja Luka at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have in your hand a book by Hasan Efendic in which he wrote, "On the first day of its renewed statehood, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina was creating or, rather, legalising the armed forces after 1884 and 1941. Bosnia has its own army once again."

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that book. I never had it in my hands, Your Honours, and I can't comment on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you confirmed at least the part that does not relate to the book but to the event, how then can you say on page 13 that the Serbs prevented the mobilisation of Muslims? Who could have prevented the mobilisation then? What prevention of mobilisation are you talking about when you see that the TO was being organised, and he himself claims that the army of BH was formed after 1887 and 1941. So what prevention of mobilisation are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a witness of what I'm going to say now is General Galic. As Colonel, he was commander of the 30th Partisan Division based in my warehouse at Kula near Mrkonjic Grad. We were attending a meeting with the president of the municipality of Donji Vakuf, Kemal Tezic, he was president of the municipality. The president of the municipality Simic Osanic [phoen] from Bugojno was also present, as well as his deputy who was president of the SDS in Bugojno. I was present and Colonel Galic. We were debating how we could calm down the situation. Also, the problem of mobilisation was discussed. And the President of the municipality of Donji Vakuf said on that occasion, Why did the Secretariat for National Defence of Donji Vakuf municipality put away the call-up papers for Muslims and Croats? And those papers were distributed only to TO conscripts who were Serb. That was the procedure applied in all other municipalities. The secretariats for national defence in which the Serbs had a much larger percentage than the others, they put away the call-up papers for Muslims and Croats so that those call-up papers were given only to Serbs. In my official notebook, I have a note from that meeting at Donji Vakuf where the president of the municipality refers to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did he say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let's clarify this. Can you give us the date of the meeting, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, for me to find it. If I can have a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it assists the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 133. I've found it. On the 13th of April, in my notebook, on page 133, it says: "PSO, president of the Municipal Assembly of Donji Vakuf, Kemal Terzic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I was going to suggest we look for it but since the witness has found it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, I don't know what the mayor of Donji Vakuf said, but do you remember that it was Izetbegovic himself who demanded that the Muslims do not respond to the call-up for mobilisation and that those who were already serving in the army should abandon the army? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never saw that document. There were comments about it, but I do not wish to comment on it because I didn't have it in my hands. There was mention of it when that document was issued and whether it was legal, whether one individual can make such a prohibition I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the whole point, that everything that was done then was done illegally. You mentioned Donji Vakuf in 1992. Do you remember that as early as the 21st of November, 1991, in the local commune of Donja Puharska, a protest rally of Muslims was organised against the decision of the legal authorities of the SFRY to implement partial mobilisation of able-bodied men of all ethnicities, of course. The Muslims were protesting because they didn't want to be drafted. And among the leadership was Dr. Mirza Mujagic, who was present president of the municipal party, and another member of the party leadership. So they protested against this partial mobilisation as early as November 1991. Do you remember that, Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I'm speaking under oath. I'm under oath, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is your regular response. You speak about Bosko Kelecevic and you say that he was directly responsible for planning and following the attack as you call it of Prijedor, Kozarac, and Derventa. How did you get that knowledge? As you say, you're under oath.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Bosko Kelecevic later General was Chief of Staff in the corps command and deputy corps commander. The Chief of Staff is the person who plans operations, and the corps commander signs them. That is what the procedure is and combat rules stipulate this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means that you derived that conclusion by deduction, not on the basis of your knowledge but on the basis of the fact that specialised bodies do the planning.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I attended meetings with the corps commander when he issued orders to his subordinates, and they noted this in official notebooks upon which they started the planning with exact deadlines who should do what by what time and then the plan would be submitted to him for signing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. So you attended decisions being taken and orders being issued regarding the attack on Prijedor, Kozarac, and Derventa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't present to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying. You couldn't be present. Is it also true that you could have no knowledge about any attack within the framework of the corridor operation in the first half of June, 1992, because you were already a pensioner by then? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not present at that, and I cannot speak about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did speak about it.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned the attack on Kozarac in 1992 and also the events in Prijedor. Do you know that in 1991 there was an event in the immediate vicinity, that is in Croatia, when the conflicts escalated and especially there were attacks on Serb villages in Western Slavonia which seriously disturbed the Serbian population living in the border area towards Croatia? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. I remember a similar situation. General Adzic ordered me when we were attending a meeting in November 1991 to tour the units of the 5th Corps together with a group of officers in Pakrac and Lipik. Colonel Talic went with me who later became corps commander. When the artillery battalion and the entire artillery was shelling the towns of Pakrac and Lipik, I watched this from an observation post. Not another shell was returned from the Croatian side. They were shelling houses. This was the order of the corps commander and Colonel Talic said it was all right, hit at them hard, and I attended this event. I was present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Selak. Now, tell me, please, that atmosphere in connection with those events and the attacks on Western Slavonia, did it prompt the Serbs from Western Slavonia to move and to flee because you were shelling them from Bosnia and Herzegovina? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not claiming that. Their Honours know why the population fled, both Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks. People were trying to save their lives. I too would have fled if I had been in their place, because in the area of combat operations, one could not be safe. And it is common knowledge who did the aggression.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You're trying to say that those Serb settlements in Western Slavonia were attacked by the Serbs, that an aggression was committed by them by your corps or as far as Bosnia and Herzegovina -- from Bosnia-Herzegovina? Is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the president of the Crisis Staff in Okucani, or rather, the commander of the TO of Okucani reported to me that there were 2.500 men present. In fact, there were 500 men. The army was arming citizens of Serb ethnicity in that area. I also have that piece of information in my notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I do hope you will answer my questions instead of responding by commenting on other matters in response to all my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The problem is that you misrepresent all the time what he's said. Now, who was it that the artillery was shelling in November 1991 when you were in Pakrac and Lipik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was close to Pakrac on the hill, at an observation post of the brigade command when Croatian towns, Pakrac and Lipik, were being shelled. And I saw both of them through binoculars, that houses were being shelled. There was a meadow in front us which was about 1 kilometre long and one could see well. There was no fire being opened against JNA units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend at that observation post?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two hours, because at 5.00 p.m. I had to be at the Mahovljani airport near Banja Luka to brief General Adzic as to what I had seen in the area of combat operations around Pakrac and Lipik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you tell him?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all I told him that the logistics had provided everything necessary for the unit and that large quantities of ammunition were being spent without cause and that we could run out of ammunition. And then for the second time that day, General Uzelac was present. He said to me -- General Uzelac's name was Nikola, and he said to him, "Nikola, you are going with Selak to Bihac. You deal with the Serbs and Osman will deal with the Turks." And I responded, "Surely you mean the Muslims, General." Both of them were quiet and he gave me a look and after that I had problems. And that was the end of my meeting with General Adzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, please, according to the SDA plan as you're talking about the municipality of Prijedor, far before the beginning of the armed conflict did the municipality of Prijedor lose a significant portion of its Muslim population? In fact, only young, able-bodied men stayed behind, and extremists representing the SDA. Do you remember that? You had the information. This was in the zone that you were in.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. In Prijedor, the majority population was Bosniak. After the 1991 elections, they should have formed the executive branch, that is the government. There were problems. And the 33rd Mechanised Brigade was in Prijedor under Colonel Arsic, and he, together with the Crisis Staff, was in charge of everything, so that the Muslims in Prijedor did not or could they have planned combat operations. Individuals and groups perhaps, but there were no military formation, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you mean only terrorist groups were being formed and not military units?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not terrorist groups but people in local communes were organising themselves using hunting weapons and what they could purchase from paramilitary formations or JNA units. And there's a list, Your Honours, in the Tribunal of the names of people who received which rifle. And I testified about that in the Brdjanin case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very, very well, Mr. Selak. But since you speak about that, do you remember that the president of the SDA in Prijedor in February 1991, president and a member of parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mirza Mujagic and President of the Municipal Assembly, Professor Muhamed Cehajic, and the secretary of the SDA, Becir Medunjanin went to the JNA barracks to protest with the officers because of the arrival of a military unit that had been dislocated there from Slovenia to Croatia or Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, a battalion arrived from Pancevo to Prijedor, the barracks there, and when the battalion was put up at the barracks, I arrived with a group of officers to see unit. It was a logistics battalion with some weaponry. Where it ended up, I don't know. But as for Mirza Mujagic and his activities, I can't speak about that because I don't have the necessary information. What I do know is that there wasn't military organisation at a larger level but just in the local communes. Now, what Mr. Mirza Mujagic himself did, I really don't know those details at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were you informed as a high-ranking officer that on the 19th of April, 1992, that the Ministry of Interior and defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina sent strictly confidential dispatches to the authorities in Prijedor with an order to block communications of military facilities to attack military units and to seize the weapons, technical materiel -- materiel and equipment? Were you informed about that in view of the fact that you were in charge of logistics, materiel, equipment, and so on as you have already explained to us?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know nothing about that document, but there is no logic to it because how can the population seize weaponry from a motorised brigade, a unit that numbered over 3.000 men?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. This was all empty -- the empty-handed population on your side. All people unarmed on your side.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Selak. Tell me this then, please, do you remember an event that took place on the 1st of May, 1992, in the night in Kozarska Street where from the back a reserve military policeman, a Serb, Radenko Capo [phoen], was killed? He was from Gornje Jelovac. And that it was known that the perpetrator was a member of the illegal paramilitary formation of the Green Berets Rahi Music nicknamed Muha [phoen]? Do you remember that event which seriously jeopardised?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. How could he remember this? It's pointless asking these questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the point is the following: It's as if you were to ask -- if I were to ask about something that took place in Scheveningen and he was here. And I asked him whether he knows what happened here. Prijedor is just by Banja Luka and in the area of his activities. So that is the analogy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us find out from the witness. Was Prijedor within your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right then. Do you remember the killing of this man called Dzapo [phoen] killed by a member of the Green Berets, Rahi Music by name?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't know the individual details and the individual cases either in Banja Luka or elsewhere. I know of many people who were killed but as to the details of the individuals I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All I'm trying to do is to try to establish together with you, Mr. Selak, the general atmosphere that prevailed at the time, because the very next day -- this happened on the 1st of May. The very next day a cousin of the person killed shot at four Muslims and then the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor expressed their condolences and regrets to the families of the people killed on both sides and appealed to the population to observe peace and calm and mutual respect, and a curfew was even introduced in order to prevent further incidents from breaking out, from 9.00 in the evening to 6:00 in the morning. I'm sure you'll remember that. That was still -- that means that was the 1st and 2nd of May, 1992. So I'm sure you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Prijedor when the battalion arrived. I have no information of that kind. They didn't reach the command of the logistics base. Whether they reached the corps, I don't know. Perhaps certain political circles, the security organs and so on, it might have reached them but the corps in Banja Luka did not get that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive the information that despite efforts made by the commune due to these two incidents, that is to say both on the Muslim side and the Serb side, that they were trying to quell the situation but what happened was quite the reverse, that during the night armed paramilitaries, Croatian ones and the SDA ones, the Party of Democratic Action in Ljubija, took control of the public security station there, disarmed and shut up the police of Serb nationality and blocked this local commune? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That piece of information is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. What about the 3rd of May, 1992? Did the leadership in the local commune of Kozarac set up an armed unit of Territorial Defence? They were actually called -- they were actually the Green Berets but they weren't called the Green Berets, and the strength was 2.500 men.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Your Honour. This is total untruth. That is absolutely not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was one of the largest formations, in actual fact, which was established at that period.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The list that the OTP has here, Your Honours, speaks of 186 or 85 men. Don't hold me to the digit. But the list stipulates exactly how many people were concerned, which weapons were issued, the number of the rifles, and 120 people were armed with some hunting rifles as well. In the entire local commune, and that served to protect the population of the Kozarac local commune in which on the 28th of May, over 2.000 people were killed in the space of one day. And allow me to say a few words about that, Your Honours, if you will, because Colonel Dragan Marcetic, for example, assistant corps commander at the time, reported as the leader of the team to the corps. And he said that on that particular day, 800 people were killed in Kozarac. General Talic looked towards me, glanced at me, because he had all -- he turned towards me, then turned towards Colonel Marcetic again, and he said, "I suppose you want to say that 80 to a hundred people were killed and you can inform the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska of that." And I have this piece of information jotted down in my notebook. There is another document in the OTP according to which the corps had reported to the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska that in fact only 80 people had been killed. Colonel Marcetic had already reduced the figure from 2000 to 800 men, whereas General Talic had ordered that the report should say that only between 80 and a hundred people had in fact been killed. And that's the truth, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, not to waste time and lose time on this you therefore claim that it is not true that in Kozarac a unit was established of the Green Berets to the strength of 3.500 men fighters; is that what you say?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I do say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that only a unit of 120 people?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: 180 to 186 was the number, the strength of the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Ah, I see. And how many inhabitants does Kozarac have?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't got the exact figures. It is a local commune, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and how many inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a local commune of Prijedor. I don't know the exact number of inhabitants. But what is true is that unit was formed to protect the local commune of Kozarac because it borders on Mount Kozara which is where the 5th Kozara Brigade had been mobilised and the commander of that brigade was Pero Colic. And that was 100 per cent Serb Territorial Defence or unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in Kozarac this wasn't a 100 per cent Muslim unit; was it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was. But it was about 175 people. Half of them didn't have weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the Serbs and Muslim were killed so the Serb brigade and the Muslim brigade and you claim that in Kozarac 2.000 people were killed, is that what you're claiming?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, come on.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there are documents to bear that out. I haven't got those documents with me, but if need be, we will find the documents with the names of the people killed and their numbers. The camp in Omarska was established at that time where the people were incarcerated. The entire population were expelled and many of these people were transferred to the Manjaca camp near Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll establish these -- it's easy to establish those facts. Just don't keep referring to the fact that they here in the OTP have those facts and figures. We know the type of facts and figures they have here. Just tell me this: At the time when these incidents were taking place in the area of the municipality of the initiative of the local population themselves, joint mixed multinational armed patrols began to be formed. This was in the village of Petrov Gaj in Trnopolje, et cetera, where there was a multi-ethnic population and similar initiatives were undertaken from different villages, from Kozarusa, for example, Cela, these are all Muslim villages. And these multinational patrols were set up to prevent the clashes and conflicts and the really tragic events that followed, that came to pass.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had no official information about that so I don't want to speak about something in general terms. I can't stand by that, so I can't answer that question, Your Honours. I can't give an explicit answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right then. What about the 10th of May in Hambarine? Was there a meeting of the leadership of the SDA that was held when the barricades were erected? I'm sure you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I am not a member of the SDA. I was an officer of the Yugoslav People's Army. As I say, I was not in Prijedor except once during the war and I can't testify about the details, about the organisation in Prijedor. I don't know. All I know is the reporting that was done to the corps commander and anything that I was able to hear from the subordinate organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you how people were killed, people who had just come to do away with the barricades, not to attack anybody, just to abolish the barricades in order to ensure the flow of traffic and they were killed? Do you remember that? All that took place at the beginning of May. You were still there in the army.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were barricades and checkpoints set up everywhere, even Banja Luka. Now, who organised those barricades, who erected them when and why I really can't say; I don't wish to comment. People organised themselves in order to protect their lives, and I can't find fault with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what you're saying is the barricades were put up, workers come to do away with the barricades, to abolish them in order to allow the free flow of traffic. And then I'm sure you'll remember in Hambarine from an ambush four members of the unit who this come to abolish the barricade were killed without attacking anybody. They didn't attack anybody. I'm sure you'll remember that.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do remember that in Hambarine there was a detainee camp which included women and children. Are they prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course they aren't, Mr. Selak. And I certainly do not consider that women and children can be considered to be prisoners of war. Tell me this now please: Was it precisely on that same day, and we're talking about May, so before the attack took place, that the authorities in Kozarac was taken over by the Red Berets and the municipality started its mobilisation and moved to work under wartime conditions? Is that how it was before the conflict that you mentioned where you say that many people were killed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Green Berets as a formation did not exist. What did exist was a Territorial Defence unit of the local commune of Kozarac with the number of people that I mentioned a moment ago. They were not the Green Berets as far as my information tells me. The official name was not the Green Berets. That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. The official title of them was not Green Berets. Now, you claim that these paramilitaries on the Serb side, that they did have an official title calling them paramilitary formations is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents to bear that out, documents belonging to the 5th Corps which mention paramilitary formations specifically and their numbers ranging between 5.100 people, although I think that the numbers were far higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Never mind. If it exists in the documents, we'll be able to find them.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you do have the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, on the 23rd of May, in Prijedor, at the crossroads between Esad Suhajlovic Street [phoen] and Miso Jasvec [phoen] Street, after these Muslim barricades, you knew Captain Mihajlo Brodo [phoen], I assume, and his associates.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know him. Unfortunately I did not know a large number of officers. Banja Luka had over 1.000 officers alone, so I couldn't know them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I won't ask you about that particular settlement then. Now, do you remember that on the 24th of May there was a clash between two different streams of the SDA, that is to say between the Muslims themselves in Kozarac and there was an armed settling of accounts in which the commander of the local Muslim paramilitary unit of the SDA was killed? His name was Osman Didovic because he considered that the time had not -- was not ripe yet for a final settling of accounts to take place, a final showdown with the authorities, the Serb authorities in the municipality?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can you ask me about details of that kind when I was in Banja Luka myself. Now, what the SDA did and the SDS or any other party in Prijedor, I really can't testify about details of that kind. I was -- never had access to those documents nor did I ask for access to them, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine, Mr. Selak. I can't ask you about any details, what happened barely 20 minutes -- 20 kilometres from where you were. You have come in here to testify against me. I was the president of a different state hundreds of kilometres away from there.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but you, Milosevic, were in command of the JNA units from June 1991, and that -- the results of that we know about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is, first of all, not true, and secondly, that's not true. And secondly, you couldn't know about any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us leave these general matters and deal with concrete matters. You've got five minutes left, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only five minutes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then I'll have to skip over many matters here and go back to the tabs. I think this particular tab was 23, tab 23. Let's just clear that point up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, it is the letter written in handwriting to the person of Mr. Momir Talic. That's what it says. The date is the 28th of May, 1993 and you quoted from that document, Mr. Selak, did you not?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we place this in the context of the material time, you will be able to see that the document speaks of something quite different in fact. Now -- so the date is indisputable. It is the end of May, the 28th of May, 1993, in fact. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you remember that on the 1st of May, the 1st and 2nd of May in Athens, the Vance-Owen Plan was signed by all three sides?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember the date [as interpreted]. I remember that the plan was signed but I can't remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now, do you remember that it was not accepted at the Assembly -- adopted at the Assembly at Pale and that because of that we introduced an embargo towards the Republika Srpska as a means of coercion and duress for them to accept the plan, the peace plan? The embargo did not only -- did not refer to humanitarian aid alone. Otherwise, all other commercial and other transactions, there was a total embargo in place. It just did not apply to humanitarian aid. Now, this particular letter shows that the deputy director of commodity reserves, deputy manager, said that according to a decision by the FRY government, nothing can be given except humanitarian aid. Is that a document which bears this out?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document shows how this official order could be bypassed, circumvented.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Whether somebody tried to bypass something or not, I cannot know myself. But I do know that thousands of tonnes of diesel fuel for the area which we -- in which we have established was inhabited by a million people necessary for hospitals and so on, the distribution of goods and food, was just a drop in the ocean. It didn't represent any great amount. And who knows how much motor oil and lubricants. So, does this document then show us when we place it in the context of the relevant material time that as a consequence of the endeavours to exert pressure for people to adopt the plan that this embargo was put in place and the commodities deputy manager says we cannot provide you with anything except humanitarian aid. Have we cleared that point up? Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we have not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then explain to me what this is about?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, when we're talking about fuel, I was eyewitness in a work organisation called Auto Servis when the fuel tanks were adapted to trailer tanks, and they were masked with tarpaulins and the fuel was transported, Your Honours, precisely in an unlawful manner, illegal manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about any smuggling.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But this is what the document speaks about, how to sidestep the provisions that were made and supply people with fuel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This is a decision of the government of the FRY to the effect that nothing can be issued, no supplies could go through except humanitarian aid. Now, whether there was smuggling going on, that's another issue altogether. That's not what I was asking you about. Let me just consult my notes for a moment. I don't know how to make the best use of the five minutes I have left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's less now. It's less now. You can ask two more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, at the end of these tabs I did not see -- I did notice this. It's 25, I think. It's tab 25. This is an order on defence securing the territory and offensive actions, command of the 1st Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you have this document before you?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What does it say here? Does it say "order"? "This is an order issued by the corps commander." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say in paragraph 2 that in the combat operations that took place so far the enemy carried out different types of genocide against the Serb people and often against their own people wishing to portray this to the international public as if it were done by the army of the SR of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, hoping for foreign intervention against the territories of the Republic of Serbian Krajina? That is the 31st of July, 1992. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says. That is what it says under the heading "Enemy," and this is an assessment of the enemy by the corps commander. Your Honours, can I say something about this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is an explanation needed?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let him answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this -- this is an assessment of the enemy. This happened regularly. The enemy would be besmirched so that the soldiers would think that they were fighting for a just cause. And it was deceptions of this kind that raised the morale of uninformed persons because they thought that this was correct information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so this is incorrect information and it is usual for the corps commander to give incorrect information?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is his assessment to a greater extent and also it's a suggestion to his own men to make this suggestion further on to the very last soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Selak, please look at page 2 of this order. Middle of the page. "Along the Svilaj-Odzak-Modrica axis, the enemy has engaged between four and five brigades of the Croatian army." So it is the Croatian army that is present in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it says the 102nd, 105th, the 106th, the 107th, the 108th Brigades. Mr. Selak, do you know that not only here but also at Kupres, for example, there was the presence of the Croatian army of Leopard tanks, German made, and so on? Do you know about that? I'm asking you whether you knew about the presence of regular Croatian army troops in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of that. And I know that the regular Croatian army entered the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina just as the Novi Sad, Valjevo and Uzice Corps entered the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and this was aggression against the sovereign State of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And I'm asking you about whether you knew about operations of these brigades and do you know about operations in the north of Bosnia-Herzegovina and down in the area of Kupres?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't know the number of brigades, but I knew that there were operations taking place. I didn't know which brigades were exactly involved, but there were operations in Kupres. The Banja Luka Corps had also sent there own men there because indeed units of the regular Croatian army were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Selak, it was my understanding that I do not have the right to put any more questions although I have quite a few left?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you had not wasted your time putting irrelevant questions which the witness can't deal with you would have had more time for the others. Yes. If you'd care to begin, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, a general matter first of all, and that is that the context of your evidence concerning what was happening within the JNA in 1990 to 1991, 1992, was at a time when certain republics of the former Yugoslavia were considering separation?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the period concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The JNA within which you served was a national institution for the former Yugoslavia, and it was being affected, just as any other institutions were, by the politics of the time. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The JNA as a national institution, like any other army, was very conscious of its historical past, the conflicts that cause it to come about and the history of the people to whom it served, and that was something that was particularly taught to officers and soldiers within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As part of that history, the events of World War II formed a very significant part of the teaching to the soldiers of the JNA, and in particular the Ustasha forces and the involvement of the axis powers?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you did not mention the Chetniks in addition to the Ustashas. They also supported the fascist forces in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. And that's a very useful observation, because throughout this institution of the JNA, as the republics were making noises and steps towards separation which would have meant the dissolution of the old Yugoslavia, a great deal of distrust was apparent within the military as people started looking towards their own ethnic groups. That's what happened?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The JNA was one of the largest armies in the world. You'll probably know better than me the full scale of that size in comparative world terms, but it was an enormous army spread throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units of the Yugoslav People's Army covered the entire territory of Yugoslavia according to strategic assessments related to the protection of the state that would come by way of aggression from neighbouring states.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
