utterances.text: Would you agree that it was an enormous army? It was probably the largest in Europe or one of the largest in Europe.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not the largest in Europe. According to the information we had, it was among the three or four best equipped and best trained armies, but whether that was actually correct or not is something I cannot say because we could not compare all of this to the other countries of Europe. This is the kind of information that we were being given, but I cannot confirm it or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well. But within the military itself, there were issues being raised as to what should happen to the army during this period of conflict between the republics, as the republics were voicing their desire to go independent.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, doesn't any state or any republic have the right to decide about its own fate? A referendum of the people or, rather, its elected Assembly has the right to think about this and to pass decisions about this. I, as a soldier, gave an oath to the Yugoslav People's Army, but the then-Yugoslav People's Army. I would have given my life for it. But in the 1990s, it what no longer that. It was no longer my army, the one that I had sworn an oath of allegiance to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the issue was that throughout the military, this was a problem for the military as to what should happen to it. Who did it belong to? Where should it go? And in 1990 and in 1991, there had been no independent creation of other armies within the separate republics?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was no organised army except in Slovenia. But the weapons of the Territorial Defence were not returned to the JNA units. The republics had the command and control over the Territorial Defence units, so the republic of Slovenia had their own units straight away, as soon as they assessed that there could be a conflict and that they should defend their state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, when you come to a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: One more question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You were a logistics officer. By any means of comparison, the JNA was a very large army. What was to happen to it had not been decided, say for a limited way in Slovenia by 1991. This institution, which was a Yugoslav institution, was still there as a whole body but with an undecided future; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Yugoslav People's Army was, in terms of its size, a major encumbrance for the economy of Yugoslavia, and I thought that the army should be downsized. However, in view of the ethnic make-up of its officers, it is quite clear why such a large army, such a strong army was held for so long, so that it could be abused by political factors, and indeed this did happen, this kind of abuse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, you gave evidence concerning the ethnic composition of the JNA, and I now want to ask you some questions about that. When you gave evidence in the Tadic case, and I'm looking at the transcript of that case at page 1827, you stated that when the first mobilisation was carried out in 1991, the ethnic composition reflected the situation on the ground. However, at the end of 1991 and 1992, this was seriously disrupted. And you went on to say the ethnic composition became 99 per cent Serb. Do you stand by that statement that the original ethnic composition reflected the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The first mobilisation was in May 1991, and it did reflect the ethnic composition on the ground from which the war units were being mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: However, in this time when certain republics were seeking their separate identity, what took place was a withdrawal of certain ethnic groups from the army.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, I'm claiming that the units in the area of Banja Luka Corps and in my area of my responsibility when the 5th Corps of the JNA was being mobilised as well as the logistic base in Banja Luka, I speak about them. I cannot talk about the ethnic composition in Slovenia, Croatia, Macedonia, and other areas because I didn't have the necessary information at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a military officer, though, of high rank involved at your level, you were aware, though, weren't you, over the situation that was developing, what the political situation was having an effect upon within the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have that information, but I'm talking about precise figures regarding the percentage of a particular ethnic group that responded to the call-up or did not respond. We had information about political developments and about the demobilisation, but I didn't have the figures by municipalities, by regions. I didn't have access to those figures nor did I need them after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not asking about the specifics in that form but the general effect. And it would be right to say that as the republics were exerting their voices and their politics to achieve independence, this was having an effect upon the composition of the army as ethnic groups sought to group together.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can say that of the reserve force that was mobilised and not of the active-duty force. The republics had authority regarding the command and equipment of TO units. If we consider the republic of Slovenia, they did not return their weapons to JNA warehouses, whereas the other republics did. So I cannot tell you exactly regarding Slovenia, how many did, how many did not, but the republics were those who had the decision-making powers according to the constitution when it came to Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the reserve, again before or at the time of 1991, the reserve officer corps corresponded in ethnic terms to the territory of each unit at that time.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how it should have been, but specifically we can't know. But in essence, yes, it did reflect in May 1991. Already by September, there was less response, and we even had to send the police to bring people to join army units, that is, the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And looking at the context of this, it again was because of the political conflict that was happening as to certain parts of the former Yugoslavia wanting to separate. It was reflecting what was happening at the political level; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the political factor that led the army. The army was an executive organ of the political powers. And this went from the level of the General Staff right down to lower-level units.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But as regards to what was happening, this was finding its way, feeling its way throughout the whole institution of the army because there was uncertainty as to what was to happen to the army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was uncertainty, and it is a question as to how the assistant commanders for moral guidance from the General Staff to the battalion, what directives they received and how they reacted. So certainly there was a dilemma as to what would happen with the whole of the JNA. I myself had dilemmas because I wasn't indifferent to it, as to what would happen tomorrow with the people and myself personally. It was only logical that we were worried about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's what I was going to ask you about next, your own experience of this matter, because you had viewed yourself as being a military officer within the Yugoslavia army?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was of a Yugoslav orientation, but I was for the equality of all nations without any domination by one nation or group or an individual over others. A life deign of man throughout the territory of Yugoslavia [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Those issue and that debate had not been resolved in 1991 or in 1992 as to what exactly was going to happen. Leaving Slovenia on one side, as to Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, whether in fact they were going to be independent states. In 1991, the early part of 1992, that had not been resolved. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatia was the first to embark upon independence. And I wouldn't like to go into that. I am speaking for Bosnia-Herzegovina. The accused, Milosevic, told me that as an officer, I was a spy -- no. I was a fighter. I would never have agreed to Muslim domination. I wanted all three nations to live on a footing of equality in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would never have played myself in the service of one nation. This is my homeland and this is my state, though this has been -- I have been accused of this. And that was my position then and still is my position now. I wish every man, every citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina to be able to live with me and to be able to move freely and lead a normal life, and this should be true of each and every citizen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving on then from that issue to the withdrawal of equipment, the withdrawal of equipment from Slovenia and Croatia in terms of the JNA made military sense at the time, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It made military sense, yes, so that the equipment and materiel should not be left to Slovenia. And everything was withdrawn. I had a question yesterday to the effect that everything was not pulled out. Everything was pulled out, even the furniture. The order of General Kadijevic, the Chief of Staff, and we have that order here, he ordered that all mobile property be withdrawn from Slovenia to Croatia, that is to Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia, and that was in fact done. And deadlines were fixed, July 1991 and October 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In military terms, no army leaves its possessions and material and equipment in a place where it may not have control over it. To you as a logistics officer, that would have made sense at the time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But that same equipment was left in Bosnia-Herzegovina and was handed to the army of Republika Srpska 100 per cent. Both the weapons in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that was withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia, and this was handed over to the army of Republika Srpska. How can that be explained?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In terms of Croatia, we have already discussed the knowledge of the military concerning historical political events, and the issues of World War II which involved Croatia were very much in the thinking of the military as to what would happen if that equipment was left in their hands. That is what they thought about it. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Normally they thought about it, indeed, but if we're saying that it was the Yugoslav People's Army, wasn't it logical for the equipment and materiel that was in Croatia, that was in Slovenia, that was in Bosnia to be left where it was instead of withdrawing everything to Bosnia-Herzegovina, Montenegro, and Serbia. So that means that is Yugoslavia. And if that was the Yugoslav army, I made a mistake as to where I was, where I served.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Exactly. This was in the context of the Yugoslavia army, because the feeling then was that there might still be a Yugoslavia in the future, that separatism may not happen, that independent states may not be created, that there was still that chance and hope that you yourself had hoped for?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once Slovenia had withdrawn and the war started in Croatia, I was sceptical that a solution would be found. Unfortunately, I was proven right, and I feared that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be a victim of those policies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As you said in your evidence in the Tadic case, and I'm looking at the transcript at page 1850: "Slovenia, Croatia slowed down the tempo of its activities so that in the meantime the Croatian people put up resistance and the formation of the Republic of Croatia took place, and a part of the weapons that was not returned was used for the struggle against the army or, rather, for the acquisition of independence." Do you -- please respond.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but let us look at Knin, Slavonia, Baranja. Weapons were distributed in an unauthorised manner to the citizens there, and that is when the fighting started. At the Plitvice lakes we know what happened, in Gospic as well. Therefore, I cannot judge the policies of the Croatian government and the Croatian people because according to the constitution they had the right to decide their own fate so I wouldn't like to enter into a polemic about that. From a military aspect, yes, but regarding political motives and solutions of the Croatian people, I would rather not, because Slovenia had a right to this and Croatia as well as a part of the federal Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But in terms of the military and the prevailing political issues, the military was aware that weapons left in places which were seeking to secede, that secession not being agreed, that those weapons could be used to achieve independence, and that's what they wanted to prevent.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who approved those political decisions? It is well known who had a majority vote in the Assembly of Yugoslavia, in the Presidency. Therefore, it is known who made the political decision. And the army was there just to carry it out. And it was abused and utilised to achieve the political goals in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to that material and equipment that was withdrawn, you've said that it was used for the replenishment of units. And in your evidence previously in Tadic and the Brdjanin case you stated you were referring to your own area of Banja Luka. "Replenishment" is a restocking of materials that were needed for the equipment of the military; is that right?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what I meant. Units of the corps in my area of responsibility and other units were 105 per cent to capacity. Five per cent were reserves. And this was provided in peacetime. There were reserve stocks in the logistic base in Banja Luka. All that came from Slovenia and Croatia entered base warehouses and was registered. However, what corps units took when the motorised transport came to the territory of Banja Luka Corps, that material was taken by the units and there was no record of that. Even General Talic spoke about that, saying it wasn't recorded. Unfortunately, that surplus, in we can call it that, was not recorded and it was distributed at will by the commander who decided to do so, whether he was brigade commander, regiment commander, or division commander. So there were never any proper records of that, how many weapons of what kind ended up where and those were surpluses. The units, Your Honours, were not entitled to have more than 5 per cent extra equipment because that would encumber them in their movement between combat operations. That is why they had a logistics base to cover all their needs on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: From the 18th of May, 1992, the command of units and bases came from that period from the Main Staff of Republika Srpska in Pale?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The decisions were officially made by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Mr. Selak, in response to a question by Mr. Milosevic, you read a quote of General Mladic of the -- and you said you -- this was from the 9th of June. I just want to simply ask you, you appear to be reading from your work notebook. Were you, in fact, reading from your work notebook which has been introduced as 463 tab 32.

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Please note that the English translation of that quote is 01104831. If I also might note there was some discussion about the work notebook with respect to an incident in Donji Vakuf. The ERN number for the translation of that portion of the workbook is 01104738. Now, Mr. Selak, during the time that General Tito was alive, was there a policy regarding the ethnic make-up of the officers' corps of the JNA reflecting the ethnic make-up of Yugoslavia in general?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was felt or, rather, it -- the commanding staff should have reflected the population or at least roughly in percentage-wise it should correspond to the ethnic composition of the population of Yugoslavia. I never had any official information up until then as to the Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 22374 to 22380. extent to which that was really properly balanced.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during the -- your cross-examination, you took out what appeared to be a printed form, and you talked about this issue, about the difference between the ethnic representation of the officer corps and the ethnic composition of Yugoslavia. I'm going to hand back a copy of that to you, and I would ask that it be assigned an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next exhibit would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 464, tab 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I might just check with the Registrar. I believe it's 46 --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you -- can you just tell us the figures that are reflected in that exhibit which you brought here with you, based upon your experience as a Colonel in the JNA, does that -- do the figures in that table represent your experience as a Colonel in the JNA during 1991?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I even thought it was even more drastic, and I was bothered by this. It troubled me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The Prosecution would be tendering that as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kay asked you a question. He have said: In military terms, no army leaves its possessions and materiel and equipment in a place where it may not have control over it, and you responded that yes, that was true. My question to you was -- or is: The assets left behind in Croatia and Bosnia, did they include air force assets of the JNA such as planes and aircraft and helicopters?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because from the Pleso airport in Zagreb, planes arrived together with all the personnel, and all the officers were relocated at the Banja Luka airport under the control of the army of Republika Srpska, and the commander of the air force was General Ninkovic, whom I knew personally. I also knew the commanders who came from Bihac and the others from the Pleso airport near Zagreb. And about 40 planes, roughly. The number varied. Some went to Belgrade. There were daily flights between Banja Luka and Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, you've testified that in the case of Slovenia, the JNA withdrew everything including tables that it owned. My question to you is: In your view as a logistics commander would it have been technically possible to have withdrawn all of the JNA property and resources from Croatia if that was the desire?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I think that from Varazdin it was not withdrawn because there was a problem. The corps commander in Varazdin was convicted in Belgrade later on. I think the armaments were left behind. The rest was pulled out even by ship, by rail, et cetera. So how much was left, I think not much because the army managed to pull out all of it at the time. Excuse me, when I was answering the gentleman's question as to whether the army should have pulled out, if it was Yugoslav, then what was in Slovenia should have been left in Slovenia. What was in Croatia should have been left in Croatia, because it was their property. The people there financed the needs of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: You refer to a case of a commander in Varazdin. Was that commander court-martialed for having left some JNA assets in Croatia that he was unauthorised to leave there?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now in the case of Bosnia, you've talked about a significant number of military assets that were left in Bosnia upon the JNA withdrawal. In your view as a logistics commander, would it have been technically possible for the JNA to have withdrawn the assets that were subsequently left in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA could have withdrawn a major portion of that equipment. It did withdraw it from all the garrisons in which the Croats and Muslims or Bosniaks were in the majority so that the Tuzla Corps was withdrawn towards Bijeljina and handed over to the army of the VRS, the 4th Corps to Pale and handed over to the VRS. Also, the Banja Luka Corps remained within the VRS. A total of five corps were formed in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the VRS using the property, the assets that were in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the assets withdrawn from Slovenia and Croatia so that they were fully replenished with all the weapons and materiel they needed. They even had a surplus.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that instead of the assets being withdrawn as they were in Slovenia, they were redistributed to areas in Bosnia where there was a predominantly Serb population?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now I'm going to be asked that you be shown Prosecution Exhibit 464, tab 23 once again. This is a document that Mr. Milosevic questioned you about this morning. My question to you is: This document is a handwritten document. It's not -- it doesn't appear on the official letterhead of the FRY government; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, at the top of that document there's a name, Amidzic. Do you know who Amidzic?

utterances.speaker: OSMAN SELAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's Bosko Amidzic, Colonel of the quatermaster service. And before that he was head of the quartermaster service in the corps. With the death of Mr. Vaso Tesic, the deputy for logistics, he took over as corps commander for logistics and that is the Amidzic who is mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now this morning Mr. Milosevic put to you the proposition that this letter taken in the context of the rejection of the Vance-Owen Plan is a clear indication that an embargo was established between the FRY and Republika Srpska. My question to you is in drawing your attention to that the sentence that reads: "It shouldn't be mentioned that this," referring to the diesel fuel, "is for the needs of the army and it will be the way that you agree." Does that sentence reflect the proposition that Mr. Milosevic put to you or more accurately reflect the proposition that soon after the embargo was put in place, that steps were being taken to circumvent it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not sure that's a proper way to put a question in re-examination, Mr. Groome. It's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will withdraw it then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at some point I think there may be some confusion over the exhibits, so if I may take stock and if the Court would like me to do that now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution in binder 464 tendered Exhibits 1, 2, 4, 6 through 16, and 19 through 23. It was our intention to withdraw the remainder. The accused in his cross-examination, however, has worked with Exhibits 3, 17, 18, and 25. The Prosecution has no objection to the introduction of those exhibits, and that would leave Exhibits 5 and 24 to be withdrawn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a technical matter. What we've just been given, these tables that Mr. Groome was commenting on, as far as I can deduce from this, these are excerpts from somebody's book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll ask the witness. Where did you get the tables from, Mr. Selak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I took these from the archives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is complete documentation about it in the research centre for the camp -- it's in -- Bosnia-Herzegovina was where I contacted somebody, and they made -- they gave me access to this. It is an authentic document, and there is documentation stored there, and we can provide it for you, Your Honours. The fact that somebody might have taken this to write a book, these facts and figures to write a book, I really can't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, is it quite clear that this is no official document? It has been and it says extracted. It is page 57, 58. So it is an excerpt of something. And in the footnotes we can see it says author Mirsad Abazovic, et cetera, and it is -- they are quotes from a book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's clarify the matter. Mr. Selak, thank you for coming to the Tribunal again to give your evidence. It is concluded and you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. There is some difficulty. Yes. Apparently there's been some confusion in the preparation of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I recall addressing the Chamber specifically two days ago saying that I was hoping to conclude Dr. Babovic and indeed one other witness today, which I was going to accomplish because I was going to take Dr. Babovic extremely shortly under the general provisions, just serving his report and tendering him for cross-examination, and I can remember saying that two days ago. And at that time, the order of witnesses was exactly as it is today and there had been notification given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be if we break early we might be able to resolve it. We've got Dr. Babovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Babovic is here and of course we're very anxious for him to be able to go home --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be that we can resolve it during the break. One thing with this witness, I would like to be clear because I don't have a curriculum vitae in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope you do now. It's tab one of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness be sworn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Budimir Babovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there's a series of exhibits associated with this witness, but might it for good order be sensible to exhibit first the expert report with its corrigendum and then following that the exhibit bundle?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, expert report will be Prosecution Exhibit 465.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May the corrigendum of the 6th of June be part of the same exhibit for convenience.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: And the binder of exhibits will be Prosecution Exhibit 466.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is one other document that I asked to be exhibited and that is -- and that is a document that's been distributed this morning which is a summary of key documents to be admitted during his testimony. I trust the Chamber's found it. It's simply a route map to remind the Chamber of what will be found in the full report should they find that convenient and if so, could that become Exhibit 467? 467 for the other exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I haven't got this route map. Where will I find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It was distributed this morning, I believe. It's a document of four pages, looks like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Summary, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dr. Babovic, did you prepare at the request of the Prosecution the report that's now been exhibited as Exhibit 465 on the police?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And your curriculum vitae at tab 1 of Exhibit 466 setting out your history and expertise, His Honour has indicated that he hasn't had an opportunity to review this in advance because no English translation was provided, so we can deal with it in a little more detail than I otherwise would have done with apologies for there not having been an English version in advance. Montenegrin by birth with a Ph.D in political science from Belgrade. You served in scientific and diplomatic institutions between 1960 and 1983, then significantly for these purposes became head of Yugoslav central bureau of INTERPOL from 1983 and until 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move on, can you explain to the Chamber what it was that caused you to retire, as you did, from that bureau in 1991?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I asked to retire ahead of time at a point in time when I realised that things were happening in the country about which nobody knew what was going on, why something was being done, who it was being done for. And apart from that, I had a clash with the people in the Ministry of the Interior too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You remained associated with INTERPOL as your CV shows, and then from 2001 became chairman of a think tank for the reform of police in Serbia, and you set out bodies of which you are an admitted member in your curriculum vitae. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've written widely. The two most significant publications perhaps for the purposes of this Trial Chamber are your book "The Police and World Order," published in Belgrade in 1997, and your book "Human Rights and Police in Yugoslavia," published in Belgrade in 1999 and 2001. Correct?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And so that there can be transparency and clarity, your book on "Human Rights and the Police in Yugoslavia," was published before you were ever contacted by the Office of the Prosecutor and indeed was probably the reason why you were contacted by them?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is precisely so. It was on the basis of the book that the OTP contacted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, unless you want me to go through the other publications, I'll leave the curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your report to which we will now turn, Exhibit 466, and I'm only going to look at half a dozen paragraphs at the most, has as its introduction at section 2, paragraph 3 on page 6, and if this could be laid on the overhead projector for -- if you've got an English-version copy, lay this page on the overhead projector I would be grateful. Contains this paragraph which I will read out, although it is the only paragraph of that size that I will read. If you could just lay the English version paragraph 3 on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's Prosecution Exhibit 465.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As part of your introductory remarks to your report, Dr. Babovic, you say this: "Throughout this period, Slobodan Milosevic had a position which de jure enabled him to directly control the highest level of the police hierarchy and thus exert a decisive influence on police organisation in Serbia. Moreover, in some respects he had an obligation to exercise control and prevent breaking of the law. During the one-party system, he was the president of the party in power, controlling all the other levers of authority which only carried out the party's will. When the multi-party system was introduced, Milosevic remained president of the Presidency, then President of the Republic of Serbia. His authority and obligations were then defined by the constitution and the laws. His position relative to the Serbian police was not weakened when he moved from the post of Serbian President to that of President of the FRY. He retained undiminished real power and acquired constitutional and legal authority because, as FRY president, he became the ex officio President of the Supreme Defence Council. In this capacity, he had legal authority over the police forces in peace and war." Help us, please. Did that paragraph draw on the documents you read and your expertise or on a combination of that and general knowledge and personal experience?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part it was based on an analysis and documents and my general knowledge and expertise and in part also the result of general analysis -- analyses which were in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As to the body of your report, I only want you to identify a couple of paragraphs where you're dependent on a single source of information so that the Chamber can have that point clearly before it. If we go to paragraph 161 on page 46. We see at this paragraph where you're dealing with the engagement of the Serbian police outside Serbia, and you use the term "para-statal formations," as inclusive of paramilitary and para-police formations. You see that you are dependent on a book footnoted at 66 by Milos Vasic and Filip Svarm. Similar reliance I think is to be found in paragraph 164. Was that book your sole source of information for the material that you're setting out in those paragraphs?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: It was the most important source of information about these issues, but of course there were other sources of information as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You could give reasons if asked why you would be prepared to rely upon Vasic and Svarm's book? I don't intend to ask you the reasons but you can give them if you are asked?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: At page -- no. We will move on then now to your conclusions which we can find at paragraph 209 on -- I think it's page 50 -- no. I beg your pardon. Page 59. If this page, paragraph 209, paragraph 210 can be laid on the overhead projector, I would be grateful. The top of the page for the usher, please. Thank you. Included in your conclusions were these, that "From 1986, Slobodan Milosevic occupied positions which de jure enabled him to directly influence the work of the organs of the interior and the violation or protection of human rights and freedoms." The analysis provided in your report focused mainly "on Kosovo and Metohija and the actions of the Serbian organs of the interior outside so-called Serbia proper. However, the manner in which the accused exercised his authority in Serbia itself should also not be forgotten." And you then end with this sentence: "Analysis has shown that de jure authority represented no boundary for Milosevic's actions. When he found it inconvenient, he would disregard it in practice or change it by issuing decrees or decisions." Does that paragraph set out in summary form the conclusions that you with your expertise reached on the analysis of the documents either already known to you or shown to you?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Paragraph 210 says this: "Milosevic not only the authority, but also the obligation to oppose violations of the laws and of human rights. If from no other provision, this obligation follows from the oaths of office he took when elected president." Do you stand by that opinion?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We pass down to paragraph 214, having covered in detail in your report the oaths he took, you find the following on analysis, "That the greatest responsibility for the most important decisions regarding the operations and conduct of the police lies with the accused."

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You then go on to say these two points. First, "That the Serbian MUP operated outside Serbia directly or through its own para-state formation and that the para-state formation established by the SDB MUPs committed crimes in the areas engulfed by the war and that Milosevic knew of the operations of the para-state formation and other MUP forces." And you refer to something that's shown on a videotape, the Chamber and you have seen, and that he approved of them, you say, but there is no proof that he asked for unlawful activities to be corrected. Here you are to some degree dealing with questions of fact, are you not?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I wasn't able to find traces of evidence of this kind that they asked that -- that he asked that unlawful activities be corrected. I found no evidence of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply draw to your attention that those paragraphs obviously are mixed in their content as to expertise and fact because we are not seeking by an expert witness to cover matters not properly in his field of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Speaking for myself, Mr. Nice, I'd like to -- I'd like the witness to reiterate the first part -- the first paragraph in this paragraph 214 and give us some reasoning and detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly. That, of course, is not a question of fact. That is a matter of expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You heard His Honour Judge Kwon's question and request. If we could go back to the first subparagraph of paragraph 214, your conclusion, the greatest responsibility for the most important decisions regarding operations and conduct of the police lay with Milosevic. Could you assist us, please, by summarising the process of reasoning that led you to that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Well, an analysis of the constitution and laws indicates that the accused was occupying positions in which those authorisations were inherent with respect to the police, whether as president of the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Serbia or as President of the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Serbia and President of Serbia by virtue of office. He had the duty and competences and authority to control, to dovetail and to guide the conduct and behaviour of the police force, and this emanates from legal provisions precisely defined and the law in 1989, and also in addition to this, it is common knowledge or, rather, the situation was well known according to which communication between the president and individual services in the Ministry of Internal Affairs was a direct communication, which means that he could directly influence decision-making on the part of these organs of state security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Babovic, much of the analysis that you did and indeed it seems to me that a great part of your conclusions would have required legal analysis, analysis of laws, am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. I am not a lawyer myself, but I did study law, and I analysed the constitution and the laws in the extent to which this was necessary for me to respond to the request made by the Tribunal for me to analyse the legal provisions and constitutional provisions from the aspects of responsibility and authority over the police. That means that although I'm not an expert in constitutional law nor am I a lawyer myself, I did limit myself to analysing those provisions in the texts which refer and regulate the police force and conduct thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But your training is not in law. It's in social science. Your expertise is not in law. It's in the social sciences.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And Dr. Babovic, having heard what you said before, may I take it that your analysis is based upon your legal knowledge as a layman or, if I can put it that way, an uncommon knowledge or common sense which is known to everybody, not based upon some factual details which you got from some documents? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have already said, I did not graduate from the faculty of law, but I did study law. So you can treat me as being a layman. You can say I'm a layman, but I don't think that that is the most suitable assessment perhaps. And in the course of my work, throughout my work, I had to confront questions where I -- which required a knowledge of certain legal provisions and constitutional provisions and stipulations, and in that sense I did gain a knowledge of the law. I apologise, but the second part of your question was what, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. And you said in addition to the legal problem, it is common knowledge or, rather, the situation was well known according to which communication between the president and individual services in the MUP. You referred to some common knowledge rather than some specific factual evidence you got some through specific evidence. Do you follow me? You based your analysis on common knowledge. Could you clarify that meaning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could, but I should first like to point out that my analysis was not based only on common knowledge and information that was accessible to all people in Yugoslavia and beyond, but I base my analysis primarily on the texts of the constitution and the appropriate laws, so that I couldn't say that my analyses were based on common knowledge and commonly held positions. They were present, but these analyses were based on a study of the constitution and the laws. And I make reference to the particular Articles of the constitution and the laws that corroborate my positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. That's what I can get as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I enlarge on what the Court has been asking you in this way: Office holders who have a connection with the police, whether President or senior policemen or junior policemen, find the scope of their powers and their duties and responsibilities identified in what material?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: The main document is the constitution which regulates in general terms, among other things, the obligations of members of the police, particularly with respect to the obligation to respect human rights, and also to preserve security and public law and order. Then comes the law on the state administration which defines the powers of individual ministries and the duties of individual ministries. Then comes the law on internal affairs which in general terms defines what needs to be done by the Ministry of Internal Affairs. And then those matters are further elaborated in the bylaws and enactments such as rules and regulations, decrees, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If we take a tangible example - I'll just find my document - to show whether police and other senior relevant ministry officials have to be acquainted with the law and its development - let me just find the one - are the examples of the laws that you've referred to and for which we have a summary that drew objection and complaint at the time that they were introduced, reflecting people's knowledge and understanding of the law?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: They did meet with criticism from professional circles at the very time they were passed. The constitution of Serbia adopted in 1990 was criticised from several different points of view. Among others, there was public criticism and the authorities recognised this need for the constitution of Serbia to be adjusted to the constitution of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that was adopted two years later. The law on internal affairs of 1989 was also criticised, especially by professional circles in the opposition because of the provisions in the first place which seriously restricted or abolished autonomy, thereby provoking additional problems. Certain rules and regulations were also criticised. For example, the law, this is not a regulation but a law, a law on ranks which in what I would call a counter constitutional manner introduced certain provisions. Shall I continue? Then certain provisions of the rules --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just pause there for a minute because there's a supplementary question I want to ask you, or two supplementary questions I want to ask you, but we'll stay with the one on ranks for a minute if we may to reflect on knowledge and, as it were, necessary expertise. If the Chamber would be good enough to go to tab 2, the summary, which is probably the easiest way of getting at it and look towards the end of the first page, number 5 and tab 5, the law on the ranks. Now, to help the Judges, your position as set out in your report is that the law on the ranks was a legitimate or an illegitimate extension of the presidential powers? You can see it in paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: There is no doubt that the law on ranks did infringe upon the constitutional principle because by a lower-level legal document matters were regulate that had could only be regulated by constitution, that is the power of the president of the republic. The law on ranks authorised the president of the republics certain -- with certain rights that were not given to him by the constitution. And as a result, this strengthened the powers of the president of the republic in relation to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was this part of the legislative developments that drew some reaction and objection? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And purely by happy coincidence, did the Serbian Constitutional Court deliver its decision on this particular piece of legislation yesterday?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And although we only have a newspaper report of its decision, its decision was to what effect?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: The decision is not identical with my analysis. I cannot say that. But basically it doesn't differ in the least from my analysis that I drew my attention to, and that is that by a lower-level legal act, matters are regulated which should be regulated by a higher-level document. And the Constitutional Court, and I have another objection regarding the law of ranks, and that is that it gave the authority to the president of the Republic of Serbia to decorate foreign citizens who have merits for the security of Serbia. And the Constitutional Court in yesterday's decision did not accept this, but I think that in the present-day situation when we have the state community of Serbia and Montenegro, this should not be accepted. However, I criticised this bearing in mind the situation when we had the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and when decorations awarded to foreign citizens was the power given to the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Dr. Babovic, you say the Constitutional Court did not accept the approach that you had to this particular question, but whose view would this Court accept? Speaking for myself, I would rather accept the Constitutional Court's position on an issue of law rather than your own, because you are bringing to this exercise your expertise as a social scientist, not as a lawyer. And it is clearly a legal issue. The question whether the law on ranks is an impermissible extension of presidential power it seems to me is quintessentially a legal issue. The Constitutional Court agreed with your point on one extent and no another way they did not agree on it and you still hold to that view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, of course I wouldn't like in any sense to call in question your own judgement that for you the position of the Constitutional Court is more relevant than mine, but I just wish to point out very briefly that the Constitutional Court did accept what was essential, and that is that the law gave powers to the president of the republic which it could not have given him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, my second supplementary question relates to the same problem, that is the need for those involved to understand the law and to be familiar with it but from a different angle. If we could go now, please, to tab 7, at least tab 7 in the summary which is on the second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just pausing there. If the witness could give us a date when the law on ranks was introduced or that provision, that Article.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. That's at tab --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: -- tab 5. And the document is dated the 26th of December, 1995, so -- and the view of the witness has been held at material times since then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: At the outset of the law it says 1879. That's why I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see what you mean. That I can't immediately explain. It's probably a copying oddity, and I don't know where 1879 comes from. It's the item number of the legislation Ms. Milenov informs me and the document itself is that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But if we could look at things from a slightly different perspective and go now to tab 7 or the summary of tab 7 on page 2 of the summary, which is the decision from the 21st of April of 1997, which was -- I beg your pardon. It's not tab 7. Absolutely my mistake. It's an exhibit that we must call from somewhere else. It's Exhibit 277. 277, please. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that exhibit is in the vault. I will get it during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But I can ask the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You reviewed a decision dated the 21st of April of 1997. Our Exhibit 277, which was a decision which identified the apparent legal right of the President of the Republic of Serbia to have direct contact with the RDB and the RDB to have the right to contact the president. Now, that, when we look at it, appears to be a formal decision, but was that something that was known publicly at the time, and when did you first learn about it?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: It was not published in public. I was aware of it at the time, but I saw the decision itself for the first time among the Tribunal's materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were aware of it, but was it generally known about at the time, or not?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Was it made available at the time, or not.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't made available to the public. And a certain smaller segment of the public did know that the head of the state security service was not communicating with the Minister or through him with the president of the republic but was communicating directly with the president of republic. The decision you are referring simply formalises such a state of affairs, makes it formal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that when we look at expertise about the police, is it necessary for somebody dealing with the police, like any policeman however junior or high, or any minister however high, is it necessary for that person to know the body of law and regulations that controls what the police do?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, but he must also follow the orders he receives from the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the second part of my question is this: Is it significant in analysing from an expert's point of view how the police were operating in fact to know what rules such as this one were made in a formal way but kept from the general public gaze?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: It is very important, because it is an indicator of a general attitude towards law and legality that existed at that time, so that when we look at that decision, it is not founded on the law on internal affairs nor in the constitution, because neither of those documents make any mention of the head of the state security service as being a collocutor of the president of the republic. Rather, it mentions either the government or the minister in the law on internal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I ask two final questions before what -- maybe the Chamber will decide is a convenient moment but if I can. The last of your conclusions at paragraph 215 says simply this: "Due to all of the above it is impossible not to raise the issue of Slobodan Milosevic's command responsibility arising from his actions or his failure to act," but is it important - I reduce my two questions to one - is it important for the learned Judges to have in mind that you're not seeking to trespass on territory they control, namely the law of this institution by interpreting command responsibility in a way that's technical to this court, but if we come back to paragraph 59 of your report, by looking at command responsibility in the way a police person would look at the issue. And you -- paragraph 59 explains how you, with your background and with your approach to the problem, view command responsibility in these terms. "Command responsibility relative to the MUPs is herein taken to mean the authority of a collective or individual state organ to issue orders to the Ministry of the Interior or within the Ministry or to directly influence its work in some other manner. Within the MUPs, command responsibility is to be found at all levels of the police hierarchy, but will be discussed here only to the level of department chief. Bearing this in mind, command responsibility in the SFRY will be discussed first." So -- did you there set out how you're using the term command responsibility in a police force.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely so. It never even occurs to me that I could suggest to this Trial Chamber any final conclusions that it will reach in this case. But I was asked to analyse the relevant documents and on that basis to present my opinion and that is what I did here. And I did so within the limits that you yourself have just indicated, Mr. Prosecutor. This is not a technical definition of command responsibility but a definition which I gave for the needs of my own analysis and report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if that's a convenient moment. I have a few more questions to ask about the summary, the route map, if I can do that, if the Chamber is going to have a break then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Milosevic, it was quite plain, and the Prosecutor made it quite plain on Wednesday that Dr. Babovic was coming after the last witness. We have the transcript here to remind us. So you should have been ready for him today. We take it there's been some confusion on your part, but it may be that during the break you can sort that out. Would you like an extra ten minutes' break in order to try to do that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, I would rather the break shouldn't be prolonged so that we don't extend the sitting. Yesterday you extended the sitting, so I had only 15 minutes for going into the fresh air, and the day before I only had five minutes. So for me, that is much more significant than when I will have the opportunity to cross-examine -- to begin cross-examining this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well, but you must be ready then to begin cross-examining this witness after the break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Mr. May, I'm ready. I never said for a moment that I wasn't ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Twenty-minute break. Dr. Babovic, could you remember in this break and any others there are, I must warn you formally, not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over, and that does include the members of the Prosecution team. Could you be back, please, in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was only -- in light of the questions that Your Honours had asked, I was only going to make some brief reference to the exhibits, but the accused being ready to cross-examine, I'm ready to maximise his time by sitting down now really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Babovic, tell me first what are you by education? You have a degree in which area?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I graduated from the faculty of philosophy, as it was called then, the group for French language and literature, and I studied law part time. Later on, I had a doctorate at the Faculty of Political Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see that you have a degree in the French language and literature. That is the diploma that you have?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And where did you get your master's degree?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: At the Faculty of Political Sciences in Belgrade in 1996, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was your master's thesis?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the master's or doctorate thesis? No. I'm sorry, I didn't have a master's thesis because the papers that I published were recognised as equivalent to the a master's degree, so I didn't have to sit for a master's degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So being by education somebody with a degree in the French language, after that you got a degree at the faculty of sciences in Belgrade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did I understand correctly from the information that I was able to glean from the documents I have that you consider yourself to be a policiologist, a police researcher. Could you explain to me what that is.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: A police researcher is a scholar that specialises in the study of the police, who studies the science of police, a science that has been in existence as such for some two decades in the world, though it is not fully and sufficiently recognised.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, at which universities in Europe is this science recognised as a science, police study?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you have a doctorate, you must know what the constituent components of any science are. Could you tell me what is a subject and what is the method of police science as a science? Because I hear of this discipline for the first time, and I should like to learn about it.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Many people haven't heard of it. As for the methods of police science, it uses the comparative and historical method. As for subject matter, it is the police, the institution of the police, its formation, development, its activities, its position in society. Those are the main determinants of that subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you get this title of police researcher?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: This is something that one doesn't acquire, this. People are the individual specialising in the police is called a policiologist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As I hear this for the first time, I assume that if there is such a science and you represent yourself as being a policiologist, then I assume you must have acquired this title as policiologist.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, but this science as such, this calling is recognised in Serbia, but it is also recognised in other countries. And at the academy of police sciences, the science of police or policiology is taught. It doesn't make any difference whether you will call it the science of police, police science, or policiology.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are aware that there are experts for the police and that there is a police academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider yourself to be an expert for the police in view of the fact that you have a degree in the French language and a doctorate at the Faculty of Political Sciences?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't say whether I consider myself that, but others do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you can't tell us whether you consider yourself to be an expert for the police.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That would be immodest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the subject of your doctorate at the Faculty of Political Sciences? What was the subject?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: International police relations and INTERPOL. That was my doctoral thesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What title did you acquire?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I acquired the title of doctor in political science.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You acquired this title of doctor of political science because you took a doctorate at that faculty. I wanted to clear that up, because I understood from Judge -- Mr. Robinson that you were a sociologist, but in fact you are a doctor in political science.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now tell me, please, in view of the fact that by education you're a teacher of French and that you have a doctorate on international police cooperation and INTERPOL, on what grounds do you consider yourself to be an expert who is qualified to explain the structure of the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia, its organisation and methods of work, the relationship between the state security and the police et cetera when you have absolutely no formal education to qualify you for this nor any real knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding that real knowledge, that is up to others to judge, but I was head of the national INTERPOL office from 1983, and surely during those activities I necessarily acquired certain knowledge about the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I assume that is what you did, as that is what it says in your biography in the Federal Secretariat for Internal Affairs. That is where you worked.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked there for about eight years; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And from what you say, you were working in -- on matters of cooperation with INTERPOL; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And as far as I know, that mainly relates to exchange of various information between the national police and INTERPOL.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is true, but when an individual engages in those activities, he may also inquire into other areas such as the work of police institutions in other countries, in his own country, various aspects of police activities and its position in society, and these were subjects that were frequently on the agenda of INTERPOL meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I gathered that as you knew French and that being one of the official languages of INTERPOL, you mainly dealt in exchange of information between our police and INTERPOL; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: From 1984 until 1991, I was in the leading bodies of INTERPOL, and for six years, from 1989 until 1992, and from 1992 until 1995, for two terms I was INTERPOL advisor for revision of the statute or constitution of INTERPOL.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in the police you did not attend any advanced additional training or seminars or the like?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that you were never involved in police operational work on the ground?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That is true too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, then, on the basis of what you, as a French teacher, consider yourself to be competent in police expertise in Serbia and Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I've already said that I cannot say that I consider myself to be competent. It is others who consider me to be competent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when were you retired, which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you get your doctorate?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Five years after you were retired?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the time when you were in the Federal Secretariat of the Interior, then Stane Dolanc was Minister of Police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: No. When I came to the federal SUP he was there but then after that there were two other ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But he brought you to the federal SUP as far as I understood things?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: He suggested that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did you do then? What were you doing then, actually, when he suggested that you come to the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Until May 1982, I was executive secretary of the Central Committee of Montenegro. When this congress was held, I did not have a job any longer, no offers were made to me. I was not told what I would do. So my friend who was president of the Yugoslav association of post and telecommunications made me an offer to head the international relations department there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Babovic. So you had held a political post in the Central Committee of the League of Communists of Montenegro and then after the congress since you were not elected you went to work in the Federal Secretariat of the Interior in view of your knowledge of the language and also in view of your political correctness?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After -- no. Actually, after that I went to work at the Yugoslav PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. You worked at the post office and then from the post office you were transferred to the federal SUP?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did you write the following paper: "Human rights and police in Yugoslavia" in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have this. Actually, it's only part of a facsimile. In that book, you claim that in Serbia, in 1997, there were about 150.000 policemen, and I assume that as author of this book you are responsible for the accuracy of the information presented in it.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I am responsible for the accuracy to the extent to which that it is known that that is what the budget appropriation was for that year. It was made public then in 1999, and it was never refuted or challenged in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Anything can be published in the newspapers. I assume that if somebody is writing a book, then one has to seek appropriate information, facts and figures. On page 83 of your book you say, that in 1997, the MUP of Serbia had about 150.000 members. That's what's written in your book. That's what you wrote; right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Babovic, do you know that in Serbia there was never more than 34.000 persons employed in the MUP? That includes the public security and the state security sectors. That is to say the uniformed police and the people who are not in uniform, the personnel not in uniform, that is to say the cooks, the typists, everybody. So altogether, it is 34.000. So why did you more than quadruple the number of personnel of the MUP? And then how does this go along with your credibility as an expert?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I said what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you get this from?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: From the newspaper, from some kind of newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some opposition newspaper, I gather?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I repeat. I've said what I have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What was your source for that figure which you gave? Could you tell us that, Dr. Babovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the source was the budget of the Republic of Serbia for that year in which a sum was appropriated for that number of police personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babovic, you know full well that the budget does not earmark personnel but finances, funds. So the only item that could have been in the budget was police expenditures. The budget would certainly not say how many members the police would have. The budget is adopted by way of a law. You know that, don't you? It's adopted by the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You don't have any other explanation?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Babovic. Tell me, is the reason for this kind of wrong exaggeration of the number of policemen in Serbia the fact that your book was published --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. He doesn't accept what you say.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't accept what you say. He says he's got the right figure and you've got the wrong one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right, Mr. May. Then perhaps I was wrong. Perhaps you are right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right tell me, please, the financing of your book, was it assisted by the Open Society Fund, the Soros fund, the one that you acknowledge in the book.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that could be seen from the book after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, it can be seen from the book. Is that the reason why you've given such figures?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: No. That never could have been the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, please, on the basis of what could you say already in the introductory part of your analysis that the police committed crimes outside Serbia and in Kosmet? What do you use to prove that? Was there a single crime that was established by a court of law on the basis of what you wrote then in that book of yours in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I don't have all the records now in front of me in terms of everything that was happening and everything that was published in the media, but I would just like to remind you that the non-governmental organisations were pointing out numerous instances of torture at police premises. They also pointed out that people died in police premises and many other unlawful actions at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. As far as unlawful actions are concerned, there can always be unlawful actions, and you could have found out about that only from criminal Prosecution of such illegal acts or perhaps some other sources.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I found out from what had been made public.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Made public where, please?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Made public in the Yugoslav media and in the foreign media. The foreign media wrote about this considerably too. Not only foreign media but also foreign state agencies also dealt with this subject matter extensively.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So you based your expertise, your expert opinion, on what you read in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: These are newspapers and people who wrote about this and who I can trust.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so that's it. And you say inter alia that the police was militarised; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know when the gendarmery was founded within the police?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, in 2001. After my term of office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The founding of the units of the gendarmery, is that militarisation of the police? Because as you said yourself, they did not exist before that.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That in itself is not an act of militarisation, because the gendarmery exists in a great many countries. And for none of these countries can one say that they have a militarised police. As for Serbia, the entire police had been militarised. There was no difference between the police and those who do not belong to the police, to the police administration.
