Everybody had ranks, everybody had weapons, everybody had light weapons, heavy weapons. And in the curriculum of the police academy, military sciences and military skills ranked first.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, that military sciences ranked first in the police academy, but ... Please, you say in your expert report on page 4, paragraph 2, that in March 2000, the Constitutional Court declared as the anti-constitutional --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. The interpreters do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Who was President of the FRY in March 2000?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: You were president.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I was president. So isn't that proof of civilian control over the legitimacy of the work of appropriate state agencies and bringing it in line with the constitution?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: We have to be reminded of the time that had to go by before an unconstitutional provision was declared as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that throughout this decision on the order on bugging this had to be -- this had to be approved by the Court of Serbia? I don't know about Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the decision to have somebody bugged would have to be approved by the Constitutional Court of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But do you know that as for both Chambers of the Federal Assembly separately and together, that is to say attached to the Chamber of citizens and also attached to the Chamber of Republics, there was a committee for security?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but I do not refer to that particular subject matter here. This ruling of the Constitutional Court is one that I refer to as proof that it was considered that a law that is not being applied -- that was not applied from when you took power was still within the legal system. It is only in that context that I referred to. I did not want to say whether there had been any bugging or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know then that throughout this time it was only the Supreme Court of Serbia that could rule on this? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You also know that in both Chambers of the Federal Assembly there were committees for defence and security respectively. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know about both. But I must say that this Constitutional Court also made certain rulings that could hardly be considered to belong to that particular area, that is to say constitutionality and legality, and this was during your rule. I can also say that one of the presidents of this -- one of the chairmen of this committee for security said officially that during his four-year term, the committee did not meet a single time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babovic, since we came to the conclusion that you're not an expert in legal matters, there is no point in going into an explanation now as to what the Constitutional Court did and whether the Constitutional Court worked according to the constitution or not. Somebody else who was qualified in legal matters would probably have to discuss that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic, you can't stop the witness giving his evidence by that sort of comment. If he wants to refer to the Constitutional Court, of course he can. Let's go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And do you know that in the National Assembly of the Republic of Serbia there was always a committee for defence and security?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that all these committees in the Assembly of Yugoslavia and in the Assembly of Serbia have the task inter alia to follow the work of the Ministry of the Interior and both of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the Republic of Serbia and therefore, the republican committee for security and defence also deals with control over the work of the ministry? So the control of work of the Ministry of the Interior also falls under that committee, that is to say of public security and of state security. The interpreters are telling me that I'm moving too fast and that I should slow down for the simultaneous interpretations. So I am trying to slow down.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: When the constitution was adopted in 1992 in the Federal Assembly and in the Republican Assembly, there was no special commission which was envisaged by law for control over the state security service. Secondly, I think that this is not a forum where we should discuss how the laws functioned and how they were observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I assume it's not, because the point of departure is that laws do function. And do you know that according to the law it is the duty of the government to submit reports on its work at least once a year to parliament? Of course including the interior as a particular area of work.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I am aware of the law, but I don't know whether the government submitted such reports every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that you are not aware of this, can that be a basis for your assertion that the government did not submit reports to the parliament and that the Ministry of the Interior within the government did not report to parliament?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: No. That can be checked.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you allege that reports were not submitted?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I'm saying, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. And do you know that it's the duty of the government to look into the lawful functioning of its own agencies?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if you know all of that, we have an example that you refer to yourself on page 4, in paragraph 2, of successful judicial control. That is what you mention in your report. And then if there is parliamentary control through appropriate parliamentary committees, how can you then claim that after the SFRY ceased to function - this is page 4, paragraph 2 - there was no control over state and public security? How can you claim that?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of knowing what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of knowing what was going on? You have judicial control and you give such an example. There are parliamentary committees and you say that there is no control because there was no control. That's what you say?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I said how this control was exercised and how a committee, the committee for defence and security, had a four-year term of office and they did not meet a single time. See then let's see what kind of control there was in fact. It was envisaged by law, but law -- the law was not enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. We have different views on that. But the control of parliament was not within my line of work, as you know. It is the executive and the legislative branches of government that are separate. Tell me what you know about this, about this in which you give your expert opinion. A policeman as a law enforcement official, does he need a special order to arrest someone, to bring someone into custody if he finds someone in the process of committing a crime?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: No, no order is needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if it is not needed, how do you explain this centralisation of the MUP to which you've made such negative references?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised that this question is being put, because the law from 1985 established in Serbia a very decentralised police system in which municipalities had very important prerogatives. Among other things, they decided who would be head of the police organisation in their own territory. They were brought together with an inter-municipal conferences or whatever these associations were called, these regional conferences. And they also had major prerogatives. In that system, the minister had the right to give an opinion about a candidate who had been put up. Now, it's not only the question of a particular candidate or head of the service. What is particularly important is that responsibility for carrying out or not carrying out duties and assignments was not geared towards the local authority where this is supposed to be carried out, or, rather, it was directed at the local authorities. And then when the law in 1989 was passed, then this was moved to the republican ministry. The republican ministry then had all powers in terms of appointing and relieving of duty all officials and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You are talking about the times of self-management and the change of the constitution when the police was organised as it was in every other country.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: What the police is organised like in other countries is a question that we can -- that can be discussed. I think that the centralisation of the police force exists in certain countries but in those countries too great efforts are being made or, rather, great efforts have been made in the past to decentralise the police and to bring the police closer to the population, to serve the population and not to serve the regime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's fine. Now, is it correct that the police, in fact, by virtue of its functions was expressly and markedly decentralised as opposed to the army where a soldier cannot act contrary or without orders from his superior in the police force according to certain situations provided by law that I quoted a moment ago. If you find someone engaged in a criminal act need not wait for anybody's order but can arrest that individual, take them into custody, et cetera. So he has been authorised. He's an authorised individual before the law and is there to enforce the law.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is not something that I'm challenging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now on page 7 of your report, paragraph 4, you say that policemen in front of the diplomatic representative offices in Belgrade, you say for years wore the uniform and insignia of the MUP of Serbia and you claim that security for those embassies came under the authority of the Federal Ministry of the Interior. Now, let's clear that point up straight away. All that is correct. It's all correct, except my question to you is: Do you know that the federal MUP, I'm talking about the Federal Ministry of the Interior, officially saw sought reinforcements from the MUP of Serbia, policemen from there because the federal MUP did not have enough men to provide security details for the diplomatic representative offices and that these same policemen which the MUP of Serbia provided to help out the federal MUP, that the federal MUP was in command of those policemen who were attached to it, because it is true that foreign representative offices was the duty of the federal MUP. It was their duty to provide security details.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, is that another example of your lack of knowledge on the subject?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think this changes matters at all because the MUP of Serbia in fact provided security details and helped out the MUP of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Babovic, have we explained this point? It was at the request of the federal MUP, in fact, that the MUP of Serbia provided to the MUP of Yugoslavia reinforcements but it was the federal MUP under whose command they came. Don't you know that?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is less important. What is more important is to see the relationship between the federal and republican MUPs, who was superior to whom and who implemented whose orders, carried out the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this, please, then: Security details for diplomatic offices and representative offices, was this done in an efficacious manner? Were these premises indeed safeguarded and protected? Were there ever any problems with regard to their security?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know that either. All right. Now do you know this: As you've been talking about the building in Kneza Milosa Street, do you know that there was a court proceedings with respect to the proprietary of the building in Kneza Milosa 92 Street and that it belonged to the MUP of Serbia and that therefore that gave them the right to enter it?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that I hear that there was a court ruling according to which the special forces of MUP were able to enter the federal offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was no violence there at all. That's got nothing to do with it. What I'm asking you -- I'm asking you because on pages 7 and 8 of your report and what you say there, do you have any valid evidence to bear that out except for the fact that you rely upon an intrigue, if I can put it that way, somebody who is allegedly my biographer and whom I don't know at all and his name is Slavoljub Djukic, somebody who wrote a book with me it seems, so you rely and refer to him. Is that the source of your expertise?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: As to that particular event I was informed after it happened, and I knew how it came to pass, how it actually happened, and that's what I write there. And I also took over an analysis provided by the recognised biographer, your recognised biographer, Slavoljub Djukic, so that I don't there's any dispute there. You say there wasn't any violence. Well, the whole hallway which is a large hall as big as this courtroom here was packed jammed with special forces with their rifles cocked at the ready. I know that from one of the men who entered with the Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Babovic. All right. We've heard that. You seem to have heard this from somebody but let's move on. And as I say, this alleged biographer I myself don't know, so I don't know how he can be any biographer of mine. Now as you claim on page 10 there was a police brigade, do you know that within the administration police department there was never a police brigade? It never existed?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Within the police administration, there was not a police brigade? Is that what you're saying? Well, we can check that out. We can verify all that, because I think that what I say is quite correct and is well-founded both on a knowledge of the rules of organisation for the MUP and also on the knowledge of the realistic state of affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we'll come to all that in due course. But as far as I remember, there was a police brigade only in the Belgrade SUP, in the SUP of the city of Belgrade and not the police administration. It never existed there. But tell me this now, please: As you claim that there were 189 departments of the interior up until the arrival of KFOR in Kosmet, and after that 110 departments of internal affairs, and you write about this on page 12, paragraph 3 of your report, is that what you're claiming? That's my question.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know that to this day there are just as many internal affairs departments as existed in 1999 and 1998 and 1995 or rather that none of them were shut down and that for the territory of Kosmet, Kosovo and Metohija, there are departments which were relocated to central Serbia but institutionally they still exist, and they perform certain activities with respect to the population, and inhabitants who had to flee under pressure of terror, under duress, they had to leave their thresholds and homes and those people of -- receiving their salaries. They have work posts that they occupy. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: In the places where the internal affairs departments existed, they no longer exist. Now, whether they exist anywhere else in paper form I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not speaking about paper and documents and chapters of any kind, I'm talking about material beings and material places and facilities, people who receive their salaries and so on and so forth. That's what I'm talking about. Let's make that clear. Now, on the basis of what are you able to claim that the other SUPs except the Belgrade SUP had as many as nine units? And you say this on page 12, paragraph 4. You say, "Apart from the Belgrade SUP, all the other SUPs had nine organisational units." That's what you state yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would help the Chamber. I think if the accused gives the actual paragraph numbers rather than the page numbers of the B/C/S because it may be the Chamber is having some trouble finding it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Paragraph number, please, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think it's about 40.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which paragraph, Mr. May?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which paragraph are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to page 12, paragraph 4 of the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Now find a number against the paragraph. Tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have that report. I have my notes in front of me, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, look, it's no good just reading out like this when no one can follow. In future if you don't have the report, make sure you note the paragraph number. Otherwise, we can't follow the cross-examination and we're likely to exclude it, nor can the witness. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can do my best to assist by -- the witness should have the B/C/S version in front of him. The page numbering and paragraph numbering is entirely different from the English version. So the fourth paragraph on page 12 would be our number -- paragraph number 40. That doesn't quite match with the line of questioning that we've been listening to but it's close to it I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are the B/C/S numbers different too?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't believe the paragraph numbers are different. It's just that the page numbers are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The paragraph numbers should be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it is not being disputed that you say that apart from the Belgrade MUP, they had nine organisational units, these other SUPs?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: That is based on access to official documents. I can't tell you now exactly which ones. I don't have them to hand. Of course I can verify this in due course later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know, for example, that in Smederevo there was a SUP with just two units, and in Velika Planinica, Smederevska Palanka, Djakovica there was just one department. In Uzice there were six units in the SUP. Priboj, Plepan [phoen], Novo Varos, Bajina Basta, Pozega and Capljina.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Well, one thing -- our organisational units that's one thing and in the local communes is quite another.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there aren't nine organisational units anywhere. So how is it you claim there were nine organisational units to each SUP department?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: According to the line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Babovic, let's move on. Let's not argue and quibble over these matters. That is not how things stand as you can see. Do you happen to know that in July 1998, by decision of the minister of the interior, Vlajko Stojiljkovic, that a staff to prevent terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was established?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I do know that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the commander of that headquarters was General Sreten Lukic; right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Sreten Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is paragraph 54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why don't you mention that in your report then?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I do mention it, precisely in paragraph 54.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you read out paragraph 54, please?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: "A month later on the 16th of June, 1998, the MUP's staff for preventing terrorism was formed and Sreten Lukic was appointed its commander too. The staff had 13 corps members including Milorad Lukovic, also known as Legija, while the expanded staff included the chiefs of the secretariats and the centre for state security from the Kosovo and Metohija area," and so on and so forth. All right. Now tell me this, please. Do you happen to know the names of the territorial organisational structures of the state security service?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: They were called the centres of state security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Centres you say?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, centres. That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, do you know that the organisation of those centres did not coincide for the most part with the organisation of the secretariats because there were far fewer centres than there were secretariats?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I write about that too. That's what I state in paragraph 56. I list all the state security centres of which there were 18 in total, whereas the secretariats of the interior, there were 32 of those. 18 and 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. How come you claim then that the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia had a command roll over the MUP of Serbia when, according to the law, the MUP of Serbia is responsible for its work to the government of Serbia and the Federal Assembly, the National Assembly?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Well, certain provisions exist, especially in the law on defence which vests the president of the SR of Yugoslavia with the power -- with these powers in peacetime, not only in times of war but the powers vested in him during peacetime as well and this relates to - I'll tell you in just a moment, let me just find it. This is implemented through the defence plan for the country which is adopted by the supreme defence council which is again led by the president of the republic whose duty it is to see to the implementation of the council's decisions and issues orders for their implementation. And the plan for the country's defence determines the rights and duties of citizens and state organs including the MUP with respect to general mobilisation, the organisation and preparations for defence as well as the commands of duties and units of the Yugoslav army in conformity with the plans and orders by -- issued by the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This means you've used deduction to conclude that a defence plan of the country is enacted in which each state organ has a role of its own to play. And on the basis of that you then go on to claim that the president of the FRY has a command responsibility over the Ministry of the Interior of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that on the basis of deduction. I'm not deducing it. I'm observing it on the basis of what has been written.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So is he in command of the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Communications, of traffic, and all the other ministries that exist in the Republic of Serbia? Because they are all state organs and by the same token they all have some role to play in the country's defence which means that the president of the FRY has a command responsibility over all these state organs. That is on the basis of what you have read out; right?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: The president decides on the deployment of the army and authorises the plan for the army's deployment and mobilisation whereas the MUP of Serbia has clearly defined tasks with respect to preparing the country's defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Babovic -- Mr. Babovic, you're quoting Article 17 very well of the law on defence which states: "That in the event of an imminent threat of war, a state of war, or a state of emergency, the units and organs of the interior may be used to carry out combat tasks, that is," and so on and so forth. The quotation is there. Those units and organs in combat tasks. These units and organs are subordinated to the Yugoslav army officer commanding the combat operations. And that is what Article 17 of the law on defence states. Is it then quite obvious, Mr. Babovic, that we're talking about concrete tasks, concrete MUP units and concrete operations on the part of the army of Yugoslavia? Now, if you don't understand it in this way, then, for example, this is what could happen: Criminal investigations during wartime should be conducted by the army, that the army should put out fires during a war, to issue passports and ID cards; right? So from this, we can see that they are subordinated exclusively to the Yugoslav army officer commanding the combat operations on the ground where they happen to be. So this refers to circumstances of that kind. It is not attachment and resubordination of the ministry to the army of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right, Mr. Babovic?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: If you read the next paragraph, then you will be able to see that we can say that the president of the Supreme Defence Council is not responsible for the manner in which these tasks and assignments are carried out. However, the supervising office in command of the combat operations cannot on his own behalf change orders and decision enacted and made by the president of the defence council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Babovic. Now, we're dealing here with imminent war operations if should they come about and resubordination exclusively within combat operations because of the principle of unity of command and not on the attachment or resubordination of the MUP to the area of responsibility. I hope that at least is clear.

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to say that this is not immediate war operations or imminent threat of -- it is an imminent threat of war, a state of war, a state of emergency. That is what it says. Those are the these stipulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll come to that too. Please. You said something in connection with Radovan Stojicic, Badza. Do you know what he became before he became Colonel General when ranks were introduced?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I heard, he was a Lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does it seem serious enough to you to give an answer as you did, as far as you heard he was a Lieutenant?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Why isn't that serious if that is what I heard from people working in the MUP and who were very embittered about it?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Babovic. Every person who doesn't think him well, but when you're compiling a report of this kind, shouldn't you check out facts so as not to give answers on the basis of what you heard? Before that in the MUP there were no ranks. So you know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There were ranks in the police -- no, the militia, the Milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But Radovan Stojicic, Badza, before acquiring that rank was the Chief Inspector, which was the highest position that existed in those days. You had from a clerk, then various types of inspectors of different ranks. His was the title of Chief Inspector. Therefore, he couldn't have been a lieutenant, nor did he have such a rank. Before that he was a commander of a special unit of public security, which again meant that he couldn't have been a Lieutenant. The least he could have been would be a Colonel. Did you have that in mind when you wrote down something like this?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: I said what I had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that when ranks were introduced he was chief of the public security department, which meant that he was in charge of the entire uniformed police?

utterances.speaker: BUDIMIR BABOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We must adjourn now at quarter to because there is another case this afternoon and the court is needed for that. Dr. Babovic, we must ask you to return, if you would, please, on Monday morning to conclude your evidence. Mr. Milosevic, you can have a further hour for cross-examination if you want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Dr. Babovic's travel plans were. I'm afraid I haven't investigated them. I hope he can be here on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, would you -- perhaps you could speak to the Prosecution about it, Dr. Babovic. If it is impossible for him to be back, then we will very have to interpose him at a later stage, but it would be much better if he could finish, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. So leave to talk to him about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Have you a list for next week? What else is coming?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have a list. I've just signed and it's ready for distribution. We've got a witness. We've overrun a bit. We've got problems and we must take witnesses as quickly as we can so that the accused must always be ready for expert witnesses to be taken with even more brevity than I took this morning's witness. I should also tell the Chamber that I'm -- I had been hoping to distribute one of the larger witness lists in an amended and updated form today. It's going to come to you, I think, on Monday. This is the list of the outstanding witnesses of all kinds including 92 bis, and it's a document that really shows the progress that we're making and the further progress by way of reduction that we're going to have to make. It should be with you on Monday or I hope, at the latest, Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So if we can we'll conclude this witness's evidence. We then have B-1407 and then Mr. Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And then of course we have got a major witness starting -- due to start on the Tuesday. It may be necessary or desirable to reorganise so that Riedlmayer comes after the following witness. I'd like the accused to have that in mind. We are intending to serve or have already served a number of exhibits that may be used with that substantial witness, although my hope is to reduce the number of exhibits that I deal with through him. My choice is between waiting until Monday, knowing precisely how limited is the exhibit base I rely on or giving the accused the opportunity to look at all the exhibits. I've gone for the later option rather than the former. We have problems about production of documents by the authorities, but I'm going to proceed without any further documents because there's no real prospect of getting them in the next day, although I have repeated my requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We will adjourn now until Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 16th day of June, 2003, at 9.00 a.m.
